packages.title: ActionSheet
packages.summary: Show the system's own action sheet and find out which option the user picked.
packages.description: Presents a list of choices in the platform's native action sheet or bottom sheet and gives you back the value of the row the user chose, or nothing if they dismissed it. You supply the rows, the title and the message, and mark destructive choices so the system styles them.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the user must choose one action from a short list, such as share, edit or delete for an item. For choosing a value in a form or a long list, use a picker or list screen instead.
packages.nativeValue: The sheet looks and behaves like the rest of the phone, with the right styling for destructive rows and the system's own dismiss gestures.

actions.description: Dismiss the current sheet, settling its show call with null. Safe when no sheet is open.

actions.name: show
actions.description: Shows the action sheet and waits. You get the value of the chosen row, or nothing when the user dismissed it.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for long lists or for choices that need typed input.

packages.title: DomActionSheet
packages.summary: Anchors native action sheets to elements inside web content.
packages.description: Converts a web element's viewport rectangle into the native window coordinates used by ActionSheet. Enable it with Dom and ActionSheet when embedded pages open anchored choices; calls and results still use the ActionSheet capability.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when embedded web content calls ActionSheet with an element rectangle. Native screens already use window coordinates, and browser-only pages need no conversion.

packages.title: Adjust
packages.summary: Find out which ad or campaign brought each install, using Adjust.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: on first launch it asks Adjust where the install came from and passes the campaign details on to your analytics destination. Needs an Adjust account and your app token. You also pick sandbox or production. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you buy installs through Adjust and want each install tied to its campaign in your analytics. Skip it if you do not use Adjust, or if probabilistic matching is on for your Adjust app and you cannot declare deterministic-only matching, because no install is attributed then.

packages.title: Google AdMob
packages.summary: Show banner, interstitial, rewarded and native ads from Google AdMob.
packages.description: Shows full-screen and rewarded ads on demand and places banner and native ads inside your screens, with the consent prompt for users who need it. You decide where and when ads appear. Needs a Google AdMob account, your AdMob App ID and an ad unit ID for each ad type you use.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to earn money from ads: call show for interstitial, rewarded or app-open ads at natural pauses, and place banner and native ads in your layout. Do not use it on the web, where AdMob is not served, or in children's apps without setting the child-directed option.

packages.title: AgeAssurance
packages.summary: Ask the phone's operating system for the user's age range.
packages.description: Uses Apple's Declared Age Range on iOS and Google's Play Age Signals on Android to learn which age band the user is in, without asking for a birthdate. Both give the same answer shape, with a yes, no or unknown result for each age you test. It asks the system to show its own prompt. You write what your app does for each age group.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you must treat under-age users differently, for example to show or hide adult content. Check for yes with a strict true test, because unknown is not the same as no. If the system cannot answer, ask for a birthdate yourself.
packages.nativeValue: The age comes from the operating system's own family and account data, which a web page cannot see.

packages.title: Airbridge
packages.summary: Attribute installs to ad campaigns and open deep links with Airbridge.
packages.description: Starts the Airbridge SDK at launch, reports which campaign led to an install and handles deferred deep links, so a new user lands on the right screen. It can wait for the iOS tracking permission decision. Needs an Airbridge account, your app name and app SDK token. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you buy ads and want to know which campaign produced each install and sale, and to send new users to the right screen through deferred deep links. Skip it if you do not use Airbridge.

packages.title: Airbridge server events
packages.summary: Send your app and web conversion events to Airbridge from your own server.
packages.description: Takes a Growth event on your server, checks that the person agreed to attribution, and sends it to the Airbridge server-to-server events API. It answers with whether it was sent and a record of the decision. You need your Airbridge app name and API token, and nothing can call it from a device.
packages.whenToUse: Send confirmed conversions to Airbridge server events from a server workflow or queue.

packages.title: Alarms and timers
packages.summary: Set alarms and timers that ring even when the phone is on silent or locked.
packages.description: Schedule one-time or repeating alarms and countdown timers, with pause, snooze and stop. On iOS 26 they ring through Silent mode and Focus and show on the Lock Screen, and on Android they take over the lock screen. Good for clock, wake-up, cooking and reminder apps. Asks the user for permission.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to build alarm clocks, timers, wake-up and reminder features that must ring even when the phone is locked or silent. For a plain reminder text, a notification is enough.

packages.title: Amplitude
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to Amplitude.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it takes the events it collects and delivers them to your Amplitude project. Use it when your team analyses behaviour in Amplitude. Needs an Amplitude account and your project API key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your team analyses behaviour in Amplitude and you already collect events with the product analytics package. It is the delivery step only; your app does not call it directly.

packages.title: Firebase Analytics
packages.summary: Send user properties and events to Google Analytics for Firebase.
packages.description: Collects nothing until you turn it on after the user agrees. Its main use is setting user properties that Firebase Remote Config targeting and Crashlytics crash-free-users numbers depend on. Needs your Firebase project set up in the app.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you need Firebase Remote Config targeting by user property, or Crashlytics crash-free-user numbers. For product analytics in general, pick one analytics tool; this package is not meant to be a second event pipe.

packages.title: Announcements
packages.summary: Show announcements in your app as a dismissible banner and a What's new list.
packages.description: Reads a feed that you own and shows the newest announcement as a banner the user can close, plus the full list as a What's new screen. Closed announcements stay closed on that device. You publish the feed and choose where the banner and list appear; nothing is shown when the feed is empty.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to tell users about new features, maintenance or incidents without shipping an update. If you only need a one-off message at launch, a simple alert is enough.

packages.title: Firebase App Check
packages.summary: Get Firebase App Check tokens so Firebase and your backend accept only your real app.
packages.description: Returns an App Check token you send in the X-Firebase-AppCheck header to Firebase services or your own backend. It relies on the App integrity check package for the device proof. iOS and Android only. Needs a Firebase project, its Web API key and your Firebase app IDs.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when Firebase services or your own backend should only answer your genuine app. Send the token in the X-Firebase-AppCheck header. It works on iOS and Android only and needs the app integrity package.

packages.title: AppClip
packages.summary: Offer a small App Clip that loads part of your app without a full install.
packages.description: Adds an iOS App Clip, a tiny version of your app that opens from a link, QR code or NFC tag and loads a web address you choose. It is off by default. You need an App Clip identifier, a link to the full app and an associated domain from Apple.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when people should be able to try a task, like paying or ordering, without installing the whole app first. If you do not plan to publish an App Clip, leave it out.

packages.title: Appearance
packages.summary: Let people choose light, dark or the system look for the whole app.
packages.description: Sets one color scheme for every part of the app at once: system bars, sheets, materials, colors and the web view. The user's choice is remembered between launches, and you can set a design default for apps that look best in only light or only dark. You build the settings control.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app offers a light, dark or automatic setting, or when your design is dark only and you want the system bars to match.

packages.title: AppGallery
packages.summary: Asks for a Huawei AppGallery rating from inside the app.
packages.description: Opt-in AppGallery review intent adapter. Calls use apprating.appgallery.request. No Huawei SDK is linked.
packages.whenToUse: Use it in an Android app distributed through Huawei AppGallery to ask for a rating there. Do not use it for Google Play or the App Store; use apprating.request.

packages.title: AppIcon
packages.summary: Let people choose the app icon shown on their home screen.
packages.description: Switches the home screen icon between the icons you declare once in your project, and tells you which icon is showing. On iOS the change is immediate with the system's own alert; on Android it applies when the app is left. You design the icons and your picker screen.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want a setting that lets people pick an app icon, such as a dark or seasonal one. It is not available on the web, and it only works with icons you declared before the build.

packages.title: Sign in with Apple
packages.summary: Let people sign in to your app with their Apple ID.
packages.description: Sign in with Apple through AuthenticationServices, Apple JS, or the Android system browser. Credentials are verified by your server.
packages.whenToUse: Use the native Apple sheet on Apple platforms, or Apple JS on web, then verify the result on your server.
packages.nativeValue: Apple platforms use the system authorization sheet and credential state notifications.

packages.title: AppLock
packages.summary: Lock your app behind Face ID, Touch ID or the device passcode.
packages.description: A biometric app lock that gates the app before any content is shown.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app shows private content, such as messages or finances, and should ask for the device owner each time it starts. It is turned on in config and has nothing to call from a page.

packages.title: AppRating
packages.summary: Ask the system to show its in-app rating prompt.
packages.description: Asks iOS or Android to show its own rating sheet inside your app, so people can rate without leaving it. The system decides whether the sheet really appears and limits how often it can, and it never tells you whether the user rated. You choose a good moment to ask.
packages.whenToUse: Use it after a moment when the user is likely to be happy, such as finishing a task. Do not attach it to a button labelled rate us, because the system may show nothing; link to your store page for that.
packages.nativeValue: The system sheet lets people leave a rating in one tap without going to the store, and the platforms keep it from being shown too often.

packages.title: Apps
packages.summary: See which Despia app surfaces are on the screen right now.
packages.description: Lets the editor page ask which Despia app surfaces, such as a side rail or a panel, are currently mounted, and whether one particular app is showing. It also holds the declarations that turn a package into an app and the host that mounts one. It runs on the web in the Studio editor only. You write the app itself.
packages.whenToUse: Use it from the editor page when you need to know what app surfaces are showing. A mounted app cannot call it on itself, and phone builds do not include it.

packages.title: App Set ID
packages.summary: Read Google Play’s current app or developer scoped identifier.
packages.description: Optional Android identifier provider. Reads the current identifier and scope on demand; never caches it. iOS callers use uuid.getNative for IDFV with different lifecycle semantics.
packages.whenToUse: Use for analytics or fraud prevention across your own Android apps, with applicable consent. Install this package explicitly to link the Google SDK.

packages.title: AppsFlyer
packages.summary: Attribute installs and purchases to ad campaigns with AppsFlyer.
packages.description: Starts the AppsFlyer SDK at launch, logs in-app events and ad revenue, reports where an install came from and resolves OneLink deep links into your app. Does nothing until a dev key is set. Needs an AppsFlyer account, your dev key and, on iOS, your Apple app ID.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you buy ads and need to know which campaign produced an install or a purchase. It does nothing until you set your AppsFlyer dev key.
packages.nativeValue: The native SDK matches installs to ad clicks and resolves OneLink deep links at the moment the app opens, which a web page cannot do.

packages.title: AppsFlyer server events
packages.summary: Send your app's conversion events to AppsFlyer from your own server.
packages.description: Takes a Growth event on your server, checks that the person agreed to attribution, and sends it to the AppsFlyer server-to-server events API. It answers with whether it was sent and a record of the decision. You need your AppsFlyer app id and S2S key, and nothing can call it from a device.
packages.whenToUse: Send confirmed conversions to AppsFlyer mobile S2S from a server workflow or queue.

packages.title: AppTracking
packages.summary: Ask the user for tracking permission and read their answer.
packages.description: Lets your app find out whether the user allows tracking and ask for it when you choose. On iOS it shows Apple's App Tracking Transparency dialog; on Android it reports the Google Play advertising ID opt-out. The framework never asks on launch, so you decide when to call it. You write the screen that explains why you ask and the code that turns tracking or personalised ads off.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app has cross-app tracking, personalised ads or attribution that depends on user consent, and you need to show the iOS tracking dialog at the right moment. Skip it if your app does no tracking, since nothing asks on launch.

result.name: identifier
result.description: The advertising identifier (IDFA or Android advertising ID) when tracking is allowed.

packages.title: App updates
packages.summary: Tell users when a newer version is available and take them to it.
packages.description: Checks whether a newer version of your app exists and lets you show an update banner. Opens the App Store sheet on iOS, and Google Play's flexible or immediate update flow on Android. Also supports installing a downloaded update. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to tell people a newer version of your app is out and send them to it. It draws no screen, so you show your own banner when the update context says one is available.

packages.title: AR
packages.summary: Run an augmented reality session on the phone camera.
packages.description: Starts an ARKit session for world tracking, face tracking or image marker tracking, and lets you place named anchors, hit-test the real world, and save and restore a mapped room. Other packages can attach their renderer to the same session. It asks for the camera the first time it starts, with text you set. You write the content that is drawn in AR.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for experiences that place things in the real world, track a face or recognise a printed marker. It is off by default because camera and AR need a clear reason in App Review.

packages.title: SceneAR
packages.summary: Place 3D scene content on real surfaces seen through the camera.
packages.description: Lets a 3D scene run in augmented reality, with the camera behind it and parts of the scene attached to flat surfaces the device finds, such as a floor or table. You write the scene and say what happens when a surface is found. It is off by default, works together with the AR package that owns the camera session, and for now only renders in AR on iOS.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when a 3D scene should appear in the person's room, for example to place furniture or a product. Skip it for ordinary 3D scenes, which need nothing extra.

packages.title: Assistants
packages.summary: Let Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight and Gemini run actions from your app.
packages.description: Turns the tools your screens declare into things system assistants can do: Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight and the Action button on iOS, and Gemini and launcher shortcuts on Android. A tool that changes something asks the person to confirm first. The shortcut files are produced at build time, so you write each tool once.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want people to say or tap a request to the phone's assistant and have your app do it, such as logging a drink or starting a timer. It cannot let an assistant change things without the person confirming.

packages.title: Meta Audience Network
packages.summary: Show full-screen Meta Audience Network ads in your app.
packages.description: Gets a bidder token from the device and shows a full-screen ad once your own bidding server returns the winning ad. Audience Network only works through server bidding, so you need that backend. Needs a Meta Audience Network account and your placement ID.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you sell full-screen ads through Meta Audience Network and already run a bidding server. It does nothing without your own server that returns a fresh winning bid for every ad.

packages.title: Audio
packages.summary: Play music, podcasts and audiobooks with lock screen controls and background playback.
packages.description: Describe what should sound and play, pause, seek and mix it. Handles the device audio session, the now-playing lock screen and remote controls, output routing and resuming where the listener left off. Use it for music, audiobooks, voice and sound effects. Works on phones and desktop.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it whenever your app makes sound: music, podcasts, audiobooks, voice, sound effects or live microphone audio. For recording to a file or editing audio use its Record and Edit children, and for video playback use the video components.

packages.title: LegacyAudioPlayer
packages.summary: Keeps the old audio:// player calls from version 3 pages working.
packages.description: Lets pages written for the version 3 native audio player keep calling audio:// links such as setqueue, play and seek, and keep receiving their events in the old window.onAudioEvent hook. It owns no player of its own and hands every call to the Audio package. New apps should call the Audio package directly and leave this out.
packages.whenToUse: Use it only when an app converted from version 3 still has pages that call audio:// links. New apps should use the Audio package directly.

packages.title: Sign-in
packages.summary: Add sign-in to your app with one set of screens and actions, whichever service holds the account.
packages.description: Gives every screen one place to read who is signed in and one set of actions for sign in, sign up, emailed codes, sign out and profile updates. Pick an account service (Despia identity, Supabase, Clerk or Firebase) and add sign-in options such as Google or Apple. Needs at least one of those packages.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app has accounts. It gives every screen the same sign-in state and actions, whichever account service you use. Skip it for apps with no sign-in.

config.label: Sign-in provider
config.description: The session provider package by name (identity, supabase, clerk). Empty picks the only one in the build.

config.label: Sign backend calls
config.description: Send the signed-in person's token with every call to your backend, refreshed when the backend says it expired. Off means calls carry only the headers you set.

packages.title: Firebase Auth
packages.summary: Sign people in with Firebase Authentication using email and password, Google or Apple.
packages.description: Keeps accounts in your Firebase project and signs people in with email and password, or with a Google or Apple credential. Gives you the Firebase ID token to check on your own server. Use it if your accounts already live in Firebase. Needs a Firebase project and its Web API key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your accounts already live in a Firebase project and you want email and password, Google or Apple sign-in. It does not offer emailed codes, phone codes or passkeys, so use another sign-in package for those.

packages.title: Despia Identity
packages.summary: Sign people in with emailed codes using your own self-hosted identity service.
packages.description: Emails a one-time code, checks it and keeps the person signed in, with no third-party account service. Use it when you want to own your user accounts. Needs the open Despia identity service deployed and its address.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want emailed one-time codes and to host your own accounts with the open identity service. If your accounts live in another service such as Firebase, Supabase or Clerk, use that package instead.

packages.title: Automotive
packages.summary: Run your app on cars that have Android built in, using Android Automotive OS.
packages.description: Adds Android Automotive OS support to the Car package. Cars with Android built in need their own app build, and this package makes that build: you export for the automotive track and the car launches your car templates directly. Include it only in the build you ship to the automotive track, since a phone build that contains it is refused. Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you ship a car app to the Android Automotive track on Google Play, for cars that run Android themselves. Skip it for phone projection through Android Auto or CarPlay, which the Car package already covers.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: The server side of LiveKit calls: it creates join tokens and receives LiveKit events.
packages.description: The secret-bearing LiveKit server half: join tokens for the verified caller and verified webhooks.
packages.whenToUse: Add it whenever your calls run on LiveKit, because the LiveKit secret must stay on your server. It has nothing to do on a device and is not used with other call providers.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: The server half of Twilio voice calls: hands out call tokens and answers Twilio's webhooks.
packages.description: Runs on your server so your Twilio secrets never ship inside the app. It creates short-lived access tokens for the signed-in caller, answers Twilio when a call starts with instructions on who to dial, and receives call status updates, checking Twilio's signature each time. You provide the Twilio settings.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you use Twilio Voice calling and need a server to sign tokens and answer Twilio. Do not call it from the app itself, because it holds secrets and only runs on a server.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: Run the small server relay that lets your app chat through Sendbird without exposing your keys.
packages.description: Gives your server a session route that creates the signed-in user's Sendbird account and a one-hour token, and a relay that passes only the allowed chat requests on to Sendbird after checking who is asking. Uploads go to your own storage bucket. You supply your Sendbird application id, API token and a relay secret, and run it on your own deployment.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you use the Sendbird chat package and need the server half that keeps your Sendbird API token off the device. It is not something the app calls directly; the chat package talks to its routes.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: The server half of Stream chat and video that keeps your Stream secret off devices.
packages.description: Runs on your own server and issues Stream user tokens for the signed-in person, creates chat channels and video calls with their members, and checks Stream's webhooks before acting on them. The chat and call packages on the device fetch their token from here. You need a Stream app with its API key and secret.
packages.whenToUse: Use it whenever you use Stream chat or video, so the Stream secret stays on your server. Skip it only if you already run your own token service.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: Let devices upload files straight to your own storage bucket with short-lived signed links.
packages.description: The server half of Files. It signs a temporary storage link for one file of the signed-in person, so the device sends the file straight to your bucket without it passing through your server and without the storage keys leaving your server. You supply the bucket and decide who may sign.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when people upload or download their own documents to your storage. Keep the lifetime short, because the link is a bearer credential. It is not for sharing files between different people.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: Receive Apple ad postbacks and mint deep links on your own server.
packages.description: The server half of Growth. It receives and verifies the attribution postbacks Apple sends for App Store ad campaigns, stores them so a workflow can read them, and creates signed deep links with short codes. It runs on your own deployment, and you supply the keys and the link domain.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you run ad campaigns on the App Store and want Apple's attribution reports, or you need to create shareable deep links that survive an install. It is server code, so it is not called from the app.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: Server-side half of device integrity: reads and writes per-device flags that survive reinstalls.
packages.description: Runs on your own server and talks to Apple DeviceCheck and Google Play Integrity. It checks a device claim sent by your app, then reads or writes a few flags tied to that physical device, such as "this device already used its free trial". Your keys stay on your server, and you decide what each flag means.
packages.whenToUse: Use it on your server to stop one device from claiming a free trial or promotion again after reinstalling. It should gate a benefit, never a sign-in.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: The server side of Stripe: payments, checkout, Connect, Identity and Issuing.
packages.description: Runs on your own server and holds your Stripe secret key. It creates the payments, setup requests, checkout sessions, keys and links that the Stripe packages in your app need, and checks Stripe's webhooks before passing events to your workflows and to commerce. You supply your Stripe keys and your catalogue prices.
packages.whenToUse: Add it whenever your app takes payments with Stripe, because the app must never hold the secret key. Skip it if you use another payment provider.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: The server side of App Store promotional offers.
packages.description: Core/Store's server half: the App Store promotional offer JWS, signed with your In-App Purchase key on your own server.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when you give subscribers an App Store promotional offer, because the offer must be signed with your private key, which belongs on your server. You do not need it for Google Play offers or for products without offers.

packages.title: Background
packages.summary: Runs your app's declared tasks in the background and tells you honestly when they ran.
packages.description: Lets you declare periodic, one-time and refresh tasks and ask the system to run them while the app is closed. Neither iOS nor Android promises exact timing, so the status report shows when each task really ran, how long it took, how it ended and why it has not run yet. You write the action each task calls.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for work that can wait and does not need exact timing, such as syncing data, uploading a queue or warming content. Do not use it for anything that must happen at a fixed time, which needs a scheduled notification or a server.

packages.title: Background Location
packages.summary: Add the declarations an app needs to track location in the background.
packages.description: Has no actions of its own. Adding it next to the location package makes the app declare background location to Apple and Google, which turns on background tracking, geofences, significant-change monitoring and visits. Leave it out if your app only asks where the person is while it is open.
packages.whenToUse: Add it only when your app tracks location in the background or uses geofences or visits, because it makes the stores treat the app as a background location app. Leave it out otherwise and the background location calls will refuse.

config.label: Background location prompt
config.description: The sentence iOS shows when the app asks to keep using location in the background. Say what happens while the app is closed, and why it is worth it.

packages.title: Base
packages.summary: A private on-device database for your app's own data, with documents, queries, backups and vector search.
packages.description: Gives the app one local database file holding key and value documents, queries over them, savepoints you can roll back, durable snapshots and a vector index for similarity search. Live queries keep a list in your screens up to date as data changes. You decide the stores and the shape of your data; nothing is sent off the device.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the app needs to store and search its own data on the device, offline and fast, including notes, caches, drafts or embeddings for search. Do not use it for data that must be shared between users; that belongs on your backend.

packages.title: Face ID and Touch ID
packages.summary: Confirm it is really the user with Face ID, Touch ID or the device passcode.
packages.description: Shows the system prompt so the user can confirm it is them with biometrics, falling back to the device passcode. Without a challenge the answer is a yes or no for the interface (a modified client can fake it, so it never protects data); pass a server challenge and the answer is a passkey assertion your server verifies. To keep a secret behind biometrics use the vault's locked records. You write the reason text shown in the prompt.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to confirm the person holding the phone before showing a screen or acting on a tap. For anything that protects data or money, pass a server challenge so your server can verify the answer.
packages.nativeValue: Face ID, Touch ID and the Android fingerprint prompt use the secure hardware and the system's own sheet, which a web page cannot reach.

actions.name: authenticate
actions.description: Shows the system Face ID, Touch ID or fingerprint prompt, falling back to the device passcode, and tells you whether the person confirmed.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to unlock a screen or confirm a sensitive tap. Add a challenge when your server must be able to trust the answer.
actions.whenNotToUse: Without a challenge, do not rely on it to protect data, money or a sign-in, because a modified app could fake the yes.

params.name: accessControl
params.description: iOS only: SecAccessControl constraints to evaluate instead of a policy. This confirms presence; it does not create or unlock a stored secret. Use IdentityVault for protected records. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: accessControlOperation
params.description: iOS only: operation for accessControl; defaults to useItem. Requires accessControl. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: allow
params.description: A list of credential ids that may answer the challenge. Used only together with challenge.

params.name: applicationPassword
params.description: iOS only: an ephemeral application credential for accessControl. Never stored or configured. Requires accessControl. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: biometricStrength
params.description: Android only: weak (default; strong when operationHandle is supplied) accepts Class 2 or Class 3 biometrics; strong requires Class 3. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: cancelTitle
params.description: iOS cancel label or Android biometric-only negative button. Android defaults to Cancel and refuses this option with a device-credential policy. Web rejects unsupported_platform.

params.name: challenge
params.description: A one-time value from your server; when given, the answer is a passkey assertion your server can verify.

params.name: confirmationRequired
params.description: Android only: request explicit confirmation after passive biometrics. Defaults to true; the OS may ignore this hint. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: description
params.description: Android only: optional prompt body. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: fallbackTitle
params.description: iOS only: localized fallback label; empty hides the fallback button. Omitted uses the OS default. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: interactionNotAllowed
params.description: iOS only: forbid authentication UI. Defaults to false. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: operationHandle
params.description: Android 15 (API 35) only: decimal signed 64-bit handle of an existing live Keystore cryptographic operation. Uses existing policy (default deviceOwner) and defaults biometricStrength to strong. Weak biometrics are invalid. Omitted uses a presence prompt. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: persistAcrossBackgrounding
params.description: Retry an OS-interrupted presence prompt on return to foreground. Defaults to false. Never retries user cancellation or a challenge ceremony.

params.name: policy
params.description: Authentication route. Defaults to deviceOwner (biometrics or passcode). deviceCredential is Android only; companion policies use iOS 18/macOS 15 APIs, with Watch policies on macOS 10.15 through 14. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: reason
params.description: The sentence shown in the prompt, for example Unlock your vault; defaults to the usage description in the package config.

params.name: reuseDuration
params.description: iOS only: seconds for reusing a recent Touch ID device unlock, from zero (default) to the OS maximum. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: rpId
params.description: The domain of your server (the relying party) that the passkey belongs to. Used together with challenge.

params.name: subtitle
params.description: Android only: optional prompt subtitle. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: timeout
params.description: Web only: WebAuthn timeout hint in milliseconds, greater than zero; defaults to 60000. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: title
params.description: Android only: prompt title. Defaults to reason. Other lanes reject unsupported_platform.

params.name: userVerification
params.description: WebAuthn user verification preference, including challenge calls on all platforms. Defaults to required. Native presence calls support required only.

result.name: assertion
result.description: The signed passkey proof your server verifies. Present only when a challenge was given and ok is true.

result.name: assertion.authenticatorData
result.description: The authenticator data that was signed, encoded as base64url.

result.name: assertion.clientDataJSON
result.description: The client data that was signed, encoded as base64url.

result.name: assertion.id
result.description: The credential id of the passkey that signed.

result.name: assertion.rawId
result.description: The raw credential id, encoded as base64url.

result.name: assertion.signature
result.description: The signature your server checks, encoded as base64url.

result.name: assertion.userHandle
result.description: The user handle stored with the passkey, when there is one.

packages.title: Block editor
packages.summary: Add a Notion-style editor where people write notes and documents in blocks.
packages.description: Type, use a slash menu for headings and lists, drag blocks around, format text and undo changes. The document is saved as markdown, so you can show it anywhere markdown is shown. Use it for notes, journals or any writing screen. No account or keys needed.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want a Notion-style writing screen for notes, journals or documents, stored as markdown. If you only need to display markdown, use the markdown element instead; if you need one plain text field, use an input.

packages.title: Bluetooth
packages.summary: Connect your app to nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices.
packages.description: Scans for Bluetooth Low Energy devices, connects, discovers services and reads, writes and subscribes to their data. Use it for wearables, sensors and other accessories. Asks for Bluetooth permission the first time it is used, with text you set. Works on phones and desktop.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to talk to Bluetooth Low Energy accessories such as heart rate straps, sensors and smart devices. It does not handle classic Bluetooth audio or pairing screens.
packages.nativeValue: Native Bluetooth scans passively, keeps connections and notifications running in the background, and replays what you missed, which Web Bluetooth cannot.

actions.name: scan
actions.description: Scans for nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices and sends a device event (with its deviceId) for each one found, until the duration ends or you stop it. On the web, where the browser only offers a device chooser, allowDuplicates and rssiThreshold are ignored and one device event fires for the pick.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to let the user choose a nearby accessory.

params.name: duration
params.description: How long to scan, in milliseconds. Defaults to 10000.

params.name: rssiThreshold
params.description: Signal strength floor in dBm, for example -80; devices weaker than this are not reported. Ignored on the web chooser.

params.name: scanMode
params.description: How aggressively Android scans: lowLatency (default), balanced or lowPower. Other platforms refuse unsupported_platform because they expose no scan scheduling mode.

params.name: services
params.description: Only report devices that advertise these service UUIDs, as a list; filtering by service is more reliable than by name.

packages.title: Branch
packages.summary: Find out which Branch link brought each install.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: on first launch it reads the Branch link that led to the install and passes the channel and campaign on to your analytics destination. Installs without a Branch link are not attributed. Needs a Branch account and your Branch key. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you run campaigns with Branch links and want to know which link brought each install. Pair it with the product analytics package, which asks for the result; it does not route deep links yet.

packages.title: Braze
packages.summary: Send events to Braze and show its push, content cards and in-app messages.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it logs your events in Braze, receives push through the Notifications package, lists content cards as data you can display and draws in-app messages. Needs a Braze account, your SDK API key and your SDK endpoint.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your marketing team runs campaigns in Braze and you want its events, push, content cards and in-app messages in your app. It needs your Braze SDK key and endpoint; without them it does nothing.

packages.title: ScreenBrightness
packages.summary: Raise or lower the screen brightness and put it back afterwards.
packages.description: Sets the screen brightness from 0 to 1, reads it, and restores the level the person had before. The original level is remembered the first time you set it and is put back automatically when the app goes to the background, so your change never outlives the app. No permission is needed. You decide when to brighten the screen.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the screen must be bright for a moment, for example to show a barcode or a QR code to a scanner. Always restore when you are done, and do not use it to dim the screen to save power.

packages.title: Browser
packages.summary: Open web links in the system's in-app browser tab.
packages.description: Opens a web address in Safari's in-app tab on iOS, a Chrome Custom Tab on Android and a new tab on the web, with the same checks everywhere. Phone, mail and other safe app links are handed to the system. Unsafe addresses such as javascript: are refused.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for links that leave your app, such as articles, terms or a payment page. For screens inside your own app, use navigation instead.
packages.nativeValue: System browser UI, saved Android browser state, and native presentation controls. iOS Safari browsing data is isolated from Safari since iOS 11; use OAuth for authentication sessions.

packages.title: Browser extension
packages.summary: Build a Chrome extension with DSX: messaging, wakes, storage, notices, side panel and tabs behind one typed API.
packages.description: Makes a browser extension a DSX target. The popup and side panel are DSX screens; the service worker and content scripts call the same typed actions, and the build writes a least-privilege manifest from the actions you use. Web only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the app you are building is a browser extension. In a native or plain web app it settles with a typed absence and does nothing.

packages.title: Bugsnag
packages.summary: Send your app's crash and error reports to your own Bugsnag project.
packages.description: Lets the error reporting package deliver its crash and error reports straight to Bugsnag over HTTPS, using your project API key. Nothing passes through Despia. It only carries the reports, while the telemetry package does the capturing, redacting and queueing.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your team already tracks errors in Bugsnag, including a self-hosted Bugsnag. You choose it as the sink when you configure telemetry.

packages.title: Calendar and reminders
packages.summary: Add events to the user's calendar and read events and reminders.
packages.description: The default opens the system event editor filled in with your event, and the user taps save, so no permission is needed. For features that need more, it can list calendars, read, create, update and remove events, and read reminders after asking permission.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when a feature needs to put an event in front of the user, such as a booking or a class, and let them save it. Use the store actions only when the app really has to read or change events itself; an app that adds one event at a time rarely needs them.

packages.title: Calls
packages.summary: Add voice and video calls that ring like real phone calls.
packages.description: Handles incoming and outgoing calls with the phone's own call screen, ringing, picture in picture and audio routing, plus ready-made call screens. It needs a call provider package (Despia, LiveKit, Twilio or Stream) to carry the audio and video.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs voice or video calls that ring and show up like real phone calls, with the lock screen call screen, picture in picture and audio routing. It carries no audio or video itself, so you also need a call provider package.

packages.title: Despia Calls
packages.summary: Carry your app's calls over WebRTC through your own Despia Calls service.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. One-to-one calls go peer to peer, and group calls go through a media server your service names. Needs the Despia Calls service deployed, plus a token endpoint on your back end.
packages.whenToUse: Use it as the call engine when you run your own Despia Calls service and want one-to-one calls to go directly between devices. You still use the calls package for the commands.

packages.title: LiveKit Calls
packages.summary: Run your app's calls and group rooms on LiveKit.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. Joins LiveKit rooms, shares microphone and camera and shows everyone's video. Needs a LiveKit server and an endpoint on your back end that issues join tokens.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your calls and group rooms to run on LiveKit. It needs the call package, a LiveKit server and a way to get a join token for each person.

packages.title: Twilio Voice
packages.summary: Make and receive voice calls with Twilio.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. Places calls to Twilio clients and receives incoming calls on the phone's call screen. Needs a Twilio account and a server that issues Twilio access tokens. Voice only, on iOS, Android and the web.
packages.whenToUse: Use it with the Calls package when your voice calls run on Twilio. Your server must mint Twilio access tokens; this package never needs your Auth Token or API secret.

packages.title: Camera
packages.summary: Capture photos and video, control a live session, and pick or save media.
packages.description: Capture photos and video through AVFoundation, CameraX or browser media APIs. Control lenses, focus, exposure, zoom, flash and torch, show a live preview, choose files with the system picker, and save captures to the photo library. Files are returned as Core/Files paths.
packages.whenToUse: Capture photos or video in code, control a live camera session, choose existing media, or save a capture to the system library.
packages.nativeValue: Uses the real camera pipelines (AVFoundation, CameraX) for low-latency capture, HDR, ProRes, RAW and lens control that a web page cannot reach.

actions.name: burst
actions.description: Takes a number of photos in a row as fast as the hardware allows, with no preview, and returns them as files.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to capture frames alongside a sensor reading or another event.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for a camera screen the person looks at; use a session with a preview instead.

actions.name: start

actions.whenNotToUse: For one-off photos call photo or burst, which open and close the camera themselves.

params.description: System camera extension to use, such as night or bokeh.

params.description: Low light boost: auto or off.

params.description: Torch level from 0 (off) to 1.

params.name: controls.whiteBalance
params.description: White balance mode, color temperature and tint.

params.description: Zoom factor to move to and how fast.

params.description: Which cameras to open, each by lens (for example back.wide) or by id; the first is the main one.

params.description: Effects applied to the picture, such as color adjustments, a LUT, blur, chroma key, overlays and guides.

params.name: mirror
params.description: Whether the picture is mirrored; the front camera is mirrored by default.

params.name: mode
params.description: What the session produces: photo, video or both.

params.name: options.aspectRatioFallback
params.description: Android fallback when the preferred photo aspect ratio is unavailable.

params.description: JPEG/HEIF compression quality, 0.01 through 1; independent of photo.quality capture priority.

params.name: options.constraints
params.description: Web getUserMedia constraints; exact/ideal/min/max are forwarded unchanged and cannot be silently relaxed.

params.description: iOS 16+ AVCaptureSession.isMultitaskingCameraAccessEnabled. Default false. True requires isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported; otherwise unsupported_config. params.description: Android ordered video qualities, including highest and lowest supported sizes.

params.description: Video size preset: sd 720x480, hd 1280x720, fhd 1920x1080, uhd 3840x2160. Cannot be combined with explicit video dimensions.

params.description: Android fallback around the last preferred video quality.

params.name: options.zeroShutterLag
params.description: Android CameraX zero shutter lag capture mode; device limitations still apply.

params.name: orientation
params.description: Which way the picture is rotated, for example following the device or locked.

params.name: photo
params.description: Photo settings: format, RAW, Live Photo, depth, quality, flash and maximum size.

params.name: photo.deferred
params.description: Let the system finish processing the photo later so the shutter returns faster.

params.description: Include depth data where the device supports it.

params.description: Flash mode: auto, on or off.

params.description: Largest photo size to capture, as width and height in pixels.

params.description: Trade speed for quality: speed, balanced or quality.

params.name: photo.raw
params.description: Also capture a RAW file where the device supports it.

params.name: video
params.description: Video settings: size, frame rate, codec, HDR, log, stabilization and bitrate.

params.description: Video codec: h264, hevc or prores.

params.description: HDR format: off, hlg, dolbyVision or hdr10.

params.description: Stabilization strength, from off to cinematic extended.

params.description: Width of the video picture in pixels.

packages.title: Capture
packages.summary: Turn any element or screen into an image, a PDF or a screen recording.
packages.description: Takes a picture of one named element, the whole app window or a component that was never shown, and writes it as a PNG, JPEG or WebP file in your app's storage. It can also make a PDF with real page sizes and record the app's own screen. Nothing goes into the photo library, and screens protected against capture are always refused. You write the markup you want captured and decide where the file goes.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to build share cards, receipts, exported pages and bug-report recordings from what your own app can draw. To put an image into the person's photo library, follow it with the media package's save.

packages.title: Car
packages.summary: Show lists, grids and messages on the car's screen with CarPlay and Android Auto.
packages.description: Takes a short car layout from your app and shows it on the vehicle's own dashboard using the templates that CarPlay and Android Auto allow: lists, grids, panes, messages and tab bars. Taps on rows come back to your app as events. Apple must grant the CarPlay entitlement for your app category before it works on a real car. You write the layout and handle the taps.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app fits a car app category such as audio, messaging or navigation and you want a simple list-based screen in the car. It cannot show custom drawings or web pages, because cars only allow their fixed templates.

packages.title: Cast to TV
packages.summary: Let users play your app's video and audio on a TV or speaker.
packages.description: Adds a cast button flow: users pick a TV or speaker and your media plays there, with play, pause, seek and queue controls. Uses AirPlay on iOS, the system output switcher on Android and Remote Playback on the web. Add the Google Cast package to also reach Chromecast and Google TV devices.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to let the person watch your video or listen to your audio on a TV or speaker. It only chooses the route; your app draws its own cast button from the context.

packages.title: ContentServer
packages.summary: Keeps the old local content server and file store working for apps converted from the previous Despia version.
packages.description: Stores files on the device, serves them to your pages through local addresses and keeps the older local CDN calls (write, read, query, delete) working. Add it when a converted app depends on them. New apps should use the Files package instead.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when converting an older Despia app that served pages or media from the local content server. For new work, use the Files package.

packages.title: Chat
packages.summary: Add messaging to your app with conversations, replies, attachments and typing.
packages.description: Gives your app conversation lists, message sending that shows at once and delivers when online, read receipts, typing indicators and attachments. It needs a chat provider package (Despia, Stream or Sendbird) to carry the messages.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to add conversations, direct messages or an assistant chat to your app, with messages that show at once and send when the device is online. It needs a chat provider package to carry the messages, and it does not draw the screens by itself.

packages.title: Despia Chat
packages.summary: Run your app's chat on your own self-hosted Despia Chat service.
packages.description: Works with the Chat package. Delivers messages live and uploads attachments directly to storage. Needs the Despia Chat service deployed and a token endpoint on your back end.
packages.whenToUse: Use it with the Chat package when you want to run messaging on your own Despia Chat service instead of a hosted chat vendor. You need to deploy that service and provide a token endpoint on your back end. If you do not want to host anything, choose a hosted chat package.

packages.title: Encrypted chat
packages.summary: Make chat messages end-to-end encrypted so only the people in the conversation can read them.
packages.description: Works with the Chat package. Encrypts each message on the sender's device and decrypts it on the others using the MLS standard, so the server never sees the text. Use it for private conversations. Needs the Chat package.
packages.whenToUse: Include it when messages must be end-to-end encrypted so even your server cannot read them. If the encryption library is not built in, encrypted sends are refused rather than sent as plain text.

packages.title: Sendbird Chat
packages.summary: Run your app's chat on Sendbird.
packages.description: Works with the Chat package. Carries messages, receipts, typing and attachments through your Sendbird application. Use it if your app already runs on Sendbird. Needs a Sendbird account and a small relay on your server that holds your Sendbird token.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app already runs its chat on Sendbird and you want the Chat package to use it. If you have no Sendbird account, pick another chat provider instead.

packages.title: Stream Chat
packages.summary: Run your app's chat on Stream.
packages.description:
Works with the Chat package. Carries messages live through your Stream app on the web, iOS and Android. Needs a Stream account, your API key and a token endpoint on your server.

![A conversation drawn by the Chat package's bubbles, carried by Stream](media/chat.png)

## What moves live

Stream's SDK keeps a connection open, so new messages, reactions, read and delivery state and the other person's typing arrive as Stream sends them. A reaction, an edit and a delete are Stream's own, and a reply is a Stream thread reply that also shows in the channel.

## Set it up

1. Create an app in the [Stream dashboard](https://getstream.io/chat/) and copy its API key and secret.
2. Add **Stream Chat** to your app. Its server half answers `POST /stream/token` for the signed-in user, so the secret never reaches the device.
3. Set `STREAM_API_KEY` and `STREAM_SECRET_KEY` as secrets of your server.
4. Open a conversation from the Chat package's screen. A conversation id is Stream's channel id, such as `messaging:general`.

## What it adds

| Target | Library | Version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web | stream-chat | 9.53.0 |
| iOS | StreamChat (Swift Package Manager) | 5.12.0 |
| Android | stream-chat-android-client | 7.12.0 |
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want the Chat package to run on your own Stream Chat account, with live messages, reactions and typing. Skip it if you use the default chat provider or another vendor.

packages.title: Clerk
packages.summary: Add sign-in, sign-up and account screens to your app with Clerk.
packages.description: Uses Clerk's native sign-in and sign-up views, email codes and social logins, and returns a session token for your own API calls. Use it if your users already live in Clerk. Needs a Clerk account and your publishable key.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your people already have Clerk accounts or you want Clerk's sign-in, social logins, passkeys, organizations and prebuilt screens. If you do not use Clerk, use the Auth package instead.
packages.nativeValue: Uses Clerk's native iOS views and Sign in with Apple, passkeys and the keychain, so sign-in feels like a system feature and works offline.

packages.title: Clipboard
packages.summary: Read from and write to the system clipboard, with a way to peek without triggering the paste alert.
packages.description: Gives you one call to read text, links, rich text, images and files from the clipboard, one to write them with options such as expiry and sensitive content, and one to check what is there without reading it. A change notification tells you when the clipboard changes. You write the buttons and screens that use it.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for copy buttons, paste buttons and share-to-clipboard features. For plain copy of a short string on a web page the browser clipboard may be enough, but this also handles images and expiry.
packages.nativeValue: Checking what is on the clipboard first avoids the system paste alert on iOS and Android, which web pages cannot do.

packages.title: Despia Commerce
packages.summary: Verify purchases and keep entitlements on your own server, with no third party in between.
packages.description: Sends every App Store and Google Play purchase to your own Despia Commerce deployment, which verifies the store's signature and keeps the entitlements. Your app then asks that server what the signed-in person owns. Works with the Store package and any sign-in provider. Needs a Despia Commerce deployment of your own.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want your own server to verify store purchases and decide what each person owns, instead of a third-party service. It does not show a payment sheet; the store package still does the buying.

packages.title: Compose
packages.summary: Opens the system text message or email composer with your message filled in, for the user to send.
packages.description: Presents the phone's own SMS or mail composer prefilled with recipients, subject, text and attachments. The user reads it and taps send themselves, so no permission is needed and the app never sends anything silently. You decide the content and when to offer the button.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for contact support, share by text or email buttons where the user should see and approve the message. To send mail from your server, use a backend instead.

packages.title: Stripe Connect
packages.summary: Put Stripe's onboarding, payouts and payments screens for connected accounts inside your platform app.
packages.description: Adds Stripe's own Connect components to your layout or as sheets, such as onboarding, payments and payouts, so sellers or providers on your platform manage their money without leaving the app. Works with the Stripe package. Needs a Stripe account with Connect, your publishable key and a server route that creates Account Sessions.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you run a platform or marketplace and want sellers or providers to onboard, see payments and manage payouts using Stripe's own screens. Your server must create account sessions. Use the main Stripe package for your own customers' payments.

packages.title: Tracking consent
packages.summary: Ask users for tracking consent and hold back analytics events until they agree.
packages.description: Stores the user's yes or no and blocks Airbridge tracking events until consent is granted. Includes a ready-made consent banner you can style or replace. It is off by default, so apps that leave it out track as before. Works with the Airbridge package.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app must get the user's permission before tracking, for example with Airbridge. Call grant after the user accepts and revoke when they change their mind. If you do not track users, leave it out.

packages.title: Console
packages.summary: See what your telemetry would send, written to the log with nothing leaving the device.
packages.description: A development destination for telemetry that prints each batch of events to the app's log instead of sending it anywhere. It makes no network requests and needs no account, so you can check exactly what a real service would receive. You choose it while wiring up a project, then switch to a real destination.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it while you set up telemetry and want to see the events before you connect a real service. It is for development, not for collecting data from users.

packages.title: Contacts
packages.summary: Let users share a contact, or read and edit the address book.
packages.description: The default is the system contact picker, which needs no permission and only returns the contact the user chooses. For features that need more, it can list, search, add, update and remove contacts and groups after asking permission, with text you set.
packages.whenToUse: Use pick when the user needs to choose one or a few people for a feature such as an invite. Only use the list, add and remove actions when the feature really needs the address book, because App Review rejects apps that ask for more than they use.
packages.nativeValue: The system picker returns only the contacts the user chooses and needs no permission, which a web page cannot match on iOS.

packages.title: Image safety check
packages.summary: Detect explicit images on the device so your content rules can hold or block them.
packages.description: Checks photos for explicit or suggestive content and passes the result to the Content policy package, which decides what to do. The image never leaves the device. On iOS it uses Apple's own detector, which respects the Sensitive Content Warning setting. Works with the Content policy package.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app lets people share photos and you want explicit images flagged on the device, before sending or after receiving. It only produces a score, and your content rules decide what happens next.

packages.title: Firebase Crashlytics
packages.summary: Report app crashes to Firebase Crashlytics.
packages.description: Uses Crashlytics as your crash reporter, with user ids, log lines and custom error records. It replaces the Error and crash reporting package's crash handler, so pick one of the two. Takes effect on the next launch. Needs your Firebase project set up in the app.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want crash reports in Firebase Crashlytics. Use it instead of the built-in crash reporter, never alongside it, because two reporters fight over the same system signals.

packages.title: Crypto
packages.summary: Hash, sign, encrypt and generate random values with the phone's own crypto.
packages.description: Gives you digests, HMAC, secure random numbers and UUIDs (v4 and time-sortable v7), plus Ed25519 and P-256 signing and AES-256-GCM encryption. Keys are created and kept in the secure store, in secure hardware when the device has it, and you only ever hold a reference. The package uses each platform's own implementation and adds no crypto of its own.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to hash or sign data, make unique ids, draw fair random numbers or encrypt small values with a key the device protects. For storing a secret between launches, use the secure storage package instead.

packages.title: Customer.io
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to Customer.io.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it delivers the events it collects to Customer.io so you can trigger messages from them. Customer.io accepts events without confirming it kept them, so check its activity log when you first connect. Needs the write key of a Customer.io browser or mobile source.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want your app's analytics events to reach Customer.io so you can trigger messages from them. Growth calls it for you after you select Customer.io; you never call it directly.

packages.title: Data
packages.summary: Declare the data tables your packages need, once, for any database you choose.
packages.description: Lets a package declare its own entities with named fields, indexes and an ownership rule, and compiles them for whichever database the build uses. Field types come from a small fixed list so the same declaration works everywhere. This package defines the schema word only; nothing in an app calls it at runtime, and you write the entities in the packages that need them.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you author a server package that stores its own records and want them created in the configured database without writing SQL or security rules. App builders who only use finished packages never need to touch it.

packages.title: Datadog
packages.summary: Send your app's error and event logs to Datadog through your own relay.
packages.description: Turns the events that Telemetry collects into Datadog log records and posts them to a relay on your own server, which forwards them to Datadog with your Datadog API key. The app never holds that key. You run the relay and choose when to turn this destination on.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you already use Datadog for logs and want crash and error events from the app to appear there. You must run an HTTPS relay that holds the API key, because Datadog says API keys must not ship in mobile or browser apps.

packages.title: DevSettings
packages.summary: A hidden developer panel for switching a test build between staging and production.
packages.description: Adds a developer panel to test installs that you open by shaking the phone. It lets testers point the same build at a staging server, scan a QR code to switch, read a live console of errors, and copy a report for support. It is switched off on App Store installs, so shipped apps never show it.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it in TestFlight and QA builds, when testers need to try your staging server without installing a different build. It does nothing in the App Store build, so it is safe to leave in.

packages.title: Device
packages.summary: Read the device, the app's own identity, the screen, locale, battery and display capabilities.
packages.description: Gives you plain answers about the phone or tablet the app runs on: hardware and OS, the app's version and first-launch state, screen size with real safe-area insets, language and region, battery and thermal state, and which hardware features exist. It needs no permission and never polls. You decide how your screens adapt to the answers.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when a screen must adapt to the device: safe-area padding, a first-launch welcome, a what's-new sheet, lighter effects on old or hot hardware, or locale-aware formatting. It does not tell you whether the user granted a permission; use the package that owns that feature.
packages.nativeValue: The numbers come straight from the OS, including real safe-area insets and screen corner radius that a web page cannot read reliably.

packages.summary: Block chosen apps and websites for a set time, on a daily schedule, or after a daily limit is used up.
packages.description: Lets the person pick apps to block, then blocks them now for a set time, every day in a time window, or once a daily limit is reached. It uses Screen Time on iOS and a blocking service on Android, with the same calls on both. You get the picker, the rules and the block screen, and you write the screens that explain why.

packages.title: Dom
packages.summary: Control the web view that shows your web app: load pages, navigate, run scripts.
packages.description: Gives you the remote control for the web view that displays your site inside the app: load a page or a bundled file, go back and forward, reload, recover after a crash, run a script, add scripts that run on every page, manage cookies and clear web data. It ships with every app and drives the web view you place in your layout. You write the pages and the calls.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your layout shows a web view and you need to steer it from buttons or code. Do not use it to pass data to new features; publish state on a package context and broadcast events instead of writing page globals.

packages.title: Downloads
packages.summary: Watch file downloads as they start, progress and finish.
packages.description: Reports the app's content downloads to your page as events when each one starts, moves forward and ends, and can list the downloads that are in flight right now. It only observes. It never starts, pauses or cancels a download, and it works for the downloads the app's content system makes itself.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want a progress bar or a done message for the app's content downloads. If you need to start or control downloads, use the Files package instead.

packages.title: Ecosystem
packages.summary: Remember a value across all of a person's own devices, with no sign-in.
packages.description: Lets a variable marked as ecosystem persist follow the person to their other devices and survive a reinstall where the platform allows. On iOS it uses iCloud, on Android a backup copy, and on the web just this browser. You choose how conflicts are settled, such as keeping the newest or the largest value.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for small preferences and progress that should follow a person without an account, such as having finished onboarding. For private data or large content, use account-based storage instead.

packages.title: Edit
packages.summary: Mixes an audio project down to a file, and measures loudness, peaks and silences in a file.
packages.description: Takes a project made of tracks and clips with trims, fades, gain, pan, effects and ducking, and renders it to a single audio file. It can also read a file and report its waveform, loudness, silences and chapters. You build the project and decide where the file goes.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for editing audio in the app, such as trimming a recording, joining clips, mixing a voice over music or evening out loudness. For simply playing audio, use the Audio package.

packages.title: ExternalApps
packages.summary: Hand a link to another app on the phone, such as Maps, Instagram or the phone dialer.
packages.description: Opens a link in the app that handles it, and does the same automatically when someone taps a link such as mailto, tel or an Instagram link. If the app is not installed it can take the person to its store page. You choose which link types are handed off in settings.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to open another app from a button or to make links like phone numbers and email addresses work. For ordinary web pages use a normal link instead.

packages.title: WatchFace
packages.summary: Show a short text and value on the watch face complication.
packages.description: Pushes one glanceable pair, such as Orders and 12, to the watchOS complication and the Wear OS tile through the Watch package. The last pair stays on the face while the watch is offline. You also need the generated watch face extension on Apple Watch.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to show one small live number or label on the watch face, such as unread orders. For richer glanceable screens, define widgets for the watch instead.

packages.title: Files
packages.summary: Save, read, download, upload and zip files in your app's own storage.
packages.description: Write a file and get a path back, list folders, copy, move, hash, zip and unzip. Large downloads and uploads keep going while the app is in the background. Use it for documents, media and cached data. An App Group ID is optional, only if you share files with extensions on iOS.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs to save, read, download or share its own files, such as exports, cached media or unpacked bundles. For small settings or records, use app data instead of files.

packages.title: FileSharing
packages.summary: Send a file to other apps through the system share sheet.
packages.description: Opens the share sheet with a file attached, so the user can send it to Messages, Mail, AirDrop, Drive, Files or any app that accepts shared files. You can share a file that is already on the device, or give an https address and the package downloads it first. Links that the server marks as attachments are shared automatically. You write the button or link that asks for the share.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the user should send, save or open a file in another app, such as a report, a ticket or an exported image. If you only want to show a link or a short text, a normal web share is enough.
packages.nativeValue: The native share sheet attaches the real file and offers every app and service on the device, which a browser cannot do reliably.

packages.title: FileViewer
packages.summary: Preview PDFs, images and documents in a native viewer.
packages.description: Opens a file in the phone's own preview screen, which handles PDFs, images, Office documents and more, or draws the same preview inside your layout. It can fetch files from an https address, including links that need the user's sign-in, and can show several files as pages to swipe through. It can also make a small thumbnail image of a file for lists. You write the screen that decides which file to show.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the user should look at a document, invoice or image without leaving the app. If you only need to send the file to another app, use the file sharing package instead.
packages.nativeValue: The native previewer renders many file types with zoom, paging and sharing built in, which a plain web view does not do well.

packages.title: DomFileViewer
packages.summary: Previews contact cards that web content downloads.
packages.description: Routes contact-card attachment downloads from embedded web content to FileViewer. It declines other attachment types so their own packages can handle them; native screens can call FileViewer directly.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your screens are web content that links to .vcf contact cards. Native screens call dsx.module.fileviewer.preview directly and do not need it.

packages.title: Firebase Cloud Messaging
packages.summary: Send push notifications to your app's users through Firebase Cloud Messaging.
packages.description: Sets up your app's Firebase identity and registers each device with Firebase Cloud Messaging, so you can send pushes from the Firebase console or your server. Use it when your team already runs on Firebase. Needs a Firebase project; on Android it asks for the Firebase App ID, API key, project ID and sender ID, and on iOS your GoogleService-Info.plist.

packages.title: Firebase Performance
packages.summary: Measure how long key flows and network requests take with Firebase Performance Monitoring.
packages.description: Works with the Error and crash reporting package: records custom timed traces such as checkout, and timings for the app's own network requests. Collection stays off until consent is granted. Needs your Firebase project set up in the app.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want to see how long key flows, such as checkout, and your own network requests take in the Firebase console. Skip it if you do not use Firebase.

packages.title: Firestore
packages.summary: Store your server data in Google Cloud Firestore and get matching access rules.
packages.description: Cloud Firestore reads, writes and live queries.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your server runs on Firebase and your data should live in Cloud Firestore. It turns your data schema into Firestore security rules and indexes. Skip it if you want Postgres, or if your server drains a work queue, which this provider does not support yet.

packages.title: Flashlight

packages.whenToUse: Use it for a torch button, a scanner light or a signal. Check availability first so you can hide the button on devices with no torch.
packages.nativeValue: The torch is driven by the device's own camera flash hardware, so it works on phones without a camera preview, which the web can only do through a live camera.

packages.title: Focus
packages.summary: Know when the app moves to the foreground or the background.
packages.description: Gives you a live value that is true while the app, or the browser tab, is in front, plus events for each change. Use it to pause video or sensors when the app goes away and resume them when it returns. There is nothing to call and no permission to ask for.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to pause or resume work that should only run while the app is visible, such as video, polling or animations. It tells you about moving between foreground and background, not about which field has the keyboard.

packages.title: Fonts
packages.summary: Use custom fonts in your app and measure text before it is drawn.
packages.description: Lets your screens use real font files at any weight, slant, variable-font axis and OpenType feature, with text that still scales with the user's accessibility size. You list the fonts your app ships, can load a themed font after launch, and can measure text for layout. You bring the font files and check their licences.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your brand needs its own typefaces, or when you need exact text widths for layout or truncation. If the system font is fine for your app, you do not need it.

packages.title: Location
packages.summary: Get the user's location, track movement and trigger geofences.
packages.description: Gets the current position, watches location changes, sets up geofences that fire when users arrive or leave, and reads compass heading and visits. Asks for permission only when a feature needs it, and you write the permission text users see. Use it for delivery, fitness and nearby offers. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when a feature depends on where the user is: showing a position, tracking a trip, firing an alert on arrival, or offering something near a store. Skip it if you only need a rough country or language, which the device locale already gives you.
packages.nativeValue: Native location gives you the operating system's own permission flow, battery-aware filtering, geofences that wake a closed app, compass heading and place visits, none of which a web page can do reliably.
