packages.title: State
packages.summary: Read, write and watch the app-wide shared store from your web page.
packages.description: Connects your web layer to the one reactive store that native screens, packages and the page all share. You can read a value by its dot-path, write one, and watch a path so your page reacts the moment anything changes it, such as sign-in, credits or theme. You decide which paths your app uses.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the web page and native parts of the app need to share live values such as the signed-in user or credits. Most apps use the dsx.global shortcuts instead of calling the actions directly; for values that belong to one page only, use that page's own variables.

packages.title: Sign in with Google
packages.summary: Let people sign in to your app with their Google account.
packages.description: Adds a Continue with Google option that uses Google's own sign-in on the web, iOS and Android, then passes the Google ID token to your account service. Needs a Google Cloud project with OAuth client ids for web and iOS, plus the reversed iOS client id as the URL scheme.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when you want a Continue with Google button in your sign-in. You call the shared sign-in with the method google; this package has no calls of its own. Skip it if your app offers no account sign-in.

packages.title: GoogleAdsConversions
packages.summary: Send purchases and sign-ups to Google Ads as conversions, from your server.
packages.description: Takes one tracked event and uploads it to Google Ads as a click conversion, matched by the ad click id or by a hashed email or phone number. It runs only on your own server, checks that the person agreed to share the data, and tells you whether the event was sent, skipped or refused. You supply your Google Ads credentials and say which conversion action each event maps to.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to report conversions that happen outside the ad click, such as a server confirmed purchase, so Google Ads can measure your campaigns. Do not call it from the app itself: it is meant for your server, and it sends nothing without recorded consent.

packages.title: Google Cast
packages.summary: Cast your app's media to Chromecast and other Google Cast TVs.
packages.description: Finds Google Cast receivers on the network, starts a session and plays and controls media on the TV. Works with the Cast to TV package, so you use the same cast calls. You can enter your own Cast receiver app id, or leave it blank to use Google's Default Media Receiver.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when you want people to play your app's video or audio on a Chromecast or other Google Cast TV. You do not call it directly: you use the Cast to TV calls and this package answers them for Google Cast receivers.

packages.title: Product analytics
packages.summary: Track what users do in your app and send it to every analytics and ad measurement tool you pick.
packages.description: Records the events you declare, such as sign-ups or checkouts, plus first open and session start automatically, and forwards them in batches to each analytics or ad measurement provider you choose, for example AppsFlyer, Meta and TikTok together. It keeps an anonymous per-install id until you identify the user, and can record where an install came from. Needs the provider packages you pick and, for some, their project token.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to measure sign-ups, purchases and where installs come from, and to send them to your analytics tool. If you only need crash reports or performance, use the monitoring packages instead.

config.label: AdAttributionKit ad network IDs
config.description: Optional, iOS publisher apps: the ad networks that may show ads in this app, as a list of lower case ids (for example "example.adattributionkit").

config.label: Allow probabilistic attribution
config.description: Off by default: only deterministic touches (a signed link, an install referrer, a referral code) are admitted. Turn on only where your privacy rules permit matching on coarse device facts.

config.label: Attribution source
config.description: Optional: the attribution row asked once for this install's touch (for example adjust). Empty means only touches the app reports through growth.attribute.

config.label: Postback copy URL
config.description: Optional, iOS: https://<your domain>. Apple then sends copies of winning postbacks to /.well-known/skadnetwork/report-attribution/ and /.well-known/appattribution/report-attribution/ on that domain, which growth.backend verifies. Apple uses only the registrable domain.

config.label: Start collecting at launch
config.description: Start sending to the chosen providers at launch, the same explicit decision as calling growth.configure.

config.label: Conversion value owner
config.description: iOS: the one package that updates Apple's conversion value (growth, appsflyer, metaads, tiktokads, airbridge, or none). The others' updates are turned off at build. Empty: your attribution source owns it when it can; two writers and no choice stop the build.

config.label: Apple conversion values
config.description: Optional, iOS: your declared events mapped to Apple's ad attribution values, for example { "signup.completed": { "fine": 10, "coarse": "low" }, "purchase.completed": { "fine": 40, "coarse": "high", "lock": true } }. fine is 0 to 63, coarse is low, medium or high, lock finalises the conversion window. Empty is off. Growth sends only a rise, and app.first_open registers the install.

config.label: Endpoints
config.description: Optional: a provider's residency host or your own proxy, by provider name. https, or http only to a local development host.

config.label: Link domain
config.description: The domain your signed deep links live on, for example links.example.com. It must be one of your app's associated domains (dsx.config.domains), so universal links and Android App Links are registered for it. Never a Despia domain.

config.label: Link public key
config.description: The Ed25519 public key (base64url, 32 bytes) that verifies your signed deep links. The matching signing key stays on your own server; the device never holds it.

config.label: Providers
config.description: The provider packages that receive every event, for example ["appsflyer", "metaads"]. Empty uses the one provider in the build; with several in the build, choose.

config.label: SKAdNetwork IDs
config.description: iOS publisher ad network identifiers. Includes Meta's two identifiers by default; replace or extend the list for your networks.

config.label: Project tokens
config.description: Each provider's public project token, by provider name, for example { "mixpanel": "<project token>" }. Never a secret key: secrets stay server-side (K8).

packages.title: LegacyGyroscope
packages.summary: Keeps old pages that read the gyroscope and compass heading working.
packages.description: Supports pages written for the earlier Despia version that start the gyroscope with the old gyroscope address and listen for its change callback. It starts the device's motion sensors at 60 readings a second and passes the old-style readings back to the page. New apps should use the Motion package directly.
packages.whenToUse: Use it only when you are keeping an older page that still calls the old gyroscope commands. For new work call the Motion package, which gives the same readings without this layer.

packages.title: Handoff
packages.summary: Let people start in your app on an iPhone and continue on a Mac or iPad.
packages.description: Advertises what the person is doing so a nearby Apple device offers to pick it up, with a web address as a fallback for devices without your app. It checks the activity type and payload size for you, because Apple fails silently when either is wrong. You decide the activity types and what small identifiers to hand over.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when a task, such as reading a recipe or editing a note, makes sense to continue on another Apple device. Hand over an identifier and fetch the rest on the other side; do not try to pass whole documents.

packages.title: Haptics
packages.summary: Add vibration feedback to taps and results.
packages.description: Touch and outcome feedback, selection changes, soft and rigid impacts, and custom patterns. Includes preparation and cancellation. No runtime permission prompt; Android VIBRATE is included automatically.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for a small physical confirmation of a touch or an outcome, such as a toggle, a saved item or a failed payment. Do not buzz on every scroll frame or for things the person cannot connect to an action.
packages.nativeValue: Uses the phone's real vibration hardware (Taptic Engine on iPhone), which a web page cannot trigger.

packages.title: WatchHealth
packages.summary: Read heart rate, steps, workouts and other health readings from the paired watch.
packages.description: Starts and stops heart rate monitoring and workouts on the user's watch, and reads today's steps, calories, distance and the latest heart rate variability, resting heart rate, oxygen and breathing readings. The watch asks the user for health permission. You decide what to show and what to do with the readings.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app should use health data recorded on the user's watch, such as a fitness or wellness feature. It needs a paired watch with your watch app installed; for health data kept on the phone, use a phone health package instead.

packages.title: Health
packages.summary: Read and write Apple Health and Android Health Connect data.
packages.description: Reads steps, heart rate, sleep and workouts, saves measurements, and can send new samples to your server in the background. The same type names work on iOS and Android, and the first read of a type asks the person for permission. Needs a health usage description for iOS; iPads and some Android phones have no health store.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your app shows or records health and fitness data on the device, or forwards it to your backend. If you want data from wearable brands through a cloud service, look at the Terra package instead.
packages.nativeValue: Talks to Apple Health and Health Connect directly with their permission sheets and background delivery, which a web page cannot reach.

packages.title: Http
packages.summary: Server routes for health checks, webhooks, live updates and a small notes example.
packages.description: Adds a set of ready-made routes to your server: a health check that reports the build, a signed webhook receiver with a retry queue and dead letters, a live update stream, and a simple notes example with a summary. It runs only on your server and has no iOS or Android code. You supply the webhook secret and decide which routes to expose.
packages.whenToUse: Use it as the starting set of server routes when you deploy your own backend, for example to check that a deployment is alive or to receive webhooks safely. Do not look for it in the app itself, since it has no native code.

packages.title: Http
packages.summary: Sends your app's error and crash reports to a web address you control, with no outside service.
packages.description: Posts each batch of telemetry as one JSON document to an https address you choose, in a documented, stable shape. A small Worker and a table are enough for complete reporting, and the data stays on your own infrastructure. You write the endpoint that receives it.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want crash and error reports on your own server instead of a vendor. If you already use a monitoring service, pick that one as the Telemetry destination instead.

packages.title: LegacyIAP
packages.summary: Keeps old v1 and v2 in-app purchase links working by answering them with the store package.
packages.description: The v3 restore verb for old WebView pages (restoreinapppurchases://), answered by Core/Store: store.restore then store.receipts, the `restored` broadcast and the v3 restore alert texts. The v1/v2 purchase verbs (inapppurchase://, inappsubscription://) were never used by v3 and are removed.
packages.whenToUse: Use it only for a converted v3 app whose pages still call the restoreinapppurchases:// link (the converter adds it, with Core/Store, when they do). Purchases and history on those pages (revenuecat://, getpurchasehistory://) are Core/Legacy rows onto Core/RevenueCat, and cancelinapppurchase:// maps to store.manage. New apps call the store package directly.

packages.title: IdentityVault
packages.summary: Stores small secrets on the device in the system keychain, with an optional Face ID or fingerprint lock.
packages.description: Writes and reads small pieces of text, such as an anonymous user id or a token, in the secure store of the device. Records can be locked so they release only after Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode, and can follow the user to a new phone through iCloud Keychain or Google Block Store. It also reports honestly how long a record will last.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for small secrets that must survive reinstalls or follow the user, such as an anonymous identity behind a purchase. Do not use it for large data or ordinary settings.
packages.nativeValue: The web has no secure store that survives, and no way to tie a value to biometrics. The keychain and hardware keys keep secrets encrypted and can bring them to a new phone.

config.label: When the vault can be read
config.description: "whenUnlocked" (default) allows reads only while the device is unlocked. "afterFirstUnlock" also allows reads while it is locked, once the user has unlocked it after a restart.

config.label: Let vault records reach the user's other devices
config.description: On by default. Records are also kept in the platform's own cross-device credential store: iCloud Keychain on iOS, Google Play Block Store on Android: so a person who buys a new phone keeps the identity they paid with. Turn it off only for a record that must stay on one device. A browser has no equivalent; the web reports that rather than pretending.

packages.title: V3 image widget
packages.summary: Keep your V3 image home-screen widget working after moving your app over from V3.
packages.description: Part of the V3 compatibility layer. The widget you set up in V3 keeps its name, so widgets people already placed survive the move. It shows an image from a link, edge to edge, and fetches it again on a refresh interval in minutes. iOS and Android only. For new apps, build widgets with the Widgets package instead.
packages.whenToUse: Use it only when converting an older Despia app that already has an image widget on people's home screens. For new widgets, use the Widgets package.

packages.title: IMessage
packages.summary: Add an iMessage app to your product that renders your own screens inside Messages.
packages.description: Builds a Messages app extension that shows your screens in the iMessage app drawer and lets people send rich cards, stickers, text and files into a conversation. Your app can also stage a card for the extension to send. You write the screens in the same layout language as the rest of your app.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your app to live inside Messages, for example to share a game move, an order or a sticker pack with friends. Skip it if you only need the standard share sheet.

packages.title: Import
packages.summary: Use an npm package from your backend code.
packages.description: Lets backend code call a real library, such as a payment SDK, without writing an import statement. You pin the npm package in the same manifest and give it a name, and your code reaches every export of it through that name. It applies to the server side only. You write the calls and handle their results.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your backend logic needs a published npm library such as a payment or email SDK. Skip it if built-in data, queue and secret features cover the job.

packages.title: App integrity check
packages.summary: Prove to your server that a request comes from a genuine, unmodified copy of your app.
packages.description: Uses Apple App Attest on iOS and Google Play Integrity on Android to produce a token your backend verifies with Apple or Google. Use it to protect your API from fake or tampered apps. Needs a server that checks the token. For iOS you pick the development or production environment in the settings.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to protect your own API from fake or tampered copies of your app: your server sends a challenge, the app returns a token, and your server checks it with Apple or Google. Do not use it to decide things inside the app, since a check run on the device can be patched.

packages.title: Intents
packages.summary: Open Android system screens and other apps by intent, and check which apps can handle one.
packages.description: Lets your app launch Android intents, which reach system settings pages that have no web address, hand a file to one specific app, or trigger a phone maker feature. It can also list the apps that could handle an intent and tell you whether any can. It does nothing on iOS or the web.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it on Android when you need a settings page such as your app's own details screen, or want to hand something to a named app. For ordinary web links use the external apps package instead.

packages.title: Intercom
packages.summary: Add Intercom's Messenger so users can chat with support, read help articles and track tickets.
packages.description: Identifies the signed-in person to Intercom, keeps their name, email and custom details current, and opens the Messenger on home, messages, help or tickets. You can also show the unread count. Needs an Intercom account, your App ID and the iOS and Android API keys, plus a server-made identity hash. iOS and Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your support team answers customers in Intercom and you want its Messenger inside your app. If you only need a simple contact form, you do not need it.

packages.title: Stripe Issuing
packages.summary: Let people add your Stripe-issued cards to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet.
packages.description: Adds an Add to Wallet button that only shows when the card and the device can take it, and shows the card number safely on the web inside Stripe's own display. Works with the Stripe package. Needs Stripe Issuing, your publishable key and server routes for card details and keys. Apple Wallet needs Apple's approval for your app; Google needs access to its TapAndPay SDK.
packages.whenToUse: Use it if you issue cards with Stripe Issuing and want cardholders to add them to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet, or see their card number safely on the web. If you only take payments, you do not need it.

packages.title: KeepAwake
packages.summary: Keep the screen from dimming or locking while something on screen needs to stay visible.
packages.description: Holds the display awake for a video, a recipe, a scanner or a map. Each screen takes its own named hold and the screen may sleep again only when the last hold is released, so two screens cannot undo each other. You can also keep the whole app awake. It draws nothing and needs no permission.
packages.whenToUse: Use it while something on screen needs to stay readable without touches, such as a video, a recipe or turn-by-turn directions. Release it when you are done so the battery is not drained.

packages.title: Keyboard
packages.summary: Ship your own system-wide iOS keyboard, drawn from your own layout.
packages.description: Adds a custom keyboard that people can turn on in iOS Settings and use in every app. It ships with a full QWERTY keyboard and you can replace its layout from your app at runtime. The keys are written in the same layout language as the rest of your app, and the keyboard can send key events back to your page.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your own keyboard, for example for emoji, stickers, templates or a branded typing experience. Skip it if you only need the normal keyboard in your own text fields.

packages.title: Kiosk
packages.summary: Lock an Android device to your app so people cannot leave it, for shared or public devices.
packages.description: Turns a company-owned Android device into a kiosk: it keeps people in your app and any other apps you allow, and can hide the status bar, the lock screen and some system buttons. It works only on Android, only after the device has been set up once so your app is its device owner, and an unlock code lets staff exit. You write the screens and choose the allowed apps.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for shared tablets, point-of-sale terminals and public displays that must stay in one app. Do not use it for ordinary consumer apps, and note it has no iOS or web version.

packages.title: V3 compatibility
packages.summary: Keep the old window.despia calls from your V3 app working after you move to V4.
packages.description: V3 pages talk to the native app with calls like window.despia = "lighthaptic://" and read old global variables and callbacks. This package catches those calls and runs them through the current packages, so your existing pages keep working without edits. Add it when moving a V3 app, and drop it once your pages use the new calls. It only covers features the other packages in your app provide.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you are moving a V3 app to V4 and your pages still call window.despia with old spellings such as lighthaptic:// or read old globals. Leave it out of new apps, and drop it once your pages use the current calls.

packages.title: LicenseCheck
packages.summary: Check your app's license on launch and show a blocking screen if it was revoked.
packages.description: Asks your own license server whether the app's license is still valid each time it starts, and shows a full-screen notice if it was revoked. A network failure never blocks, so an offline phone keeps working. It stays dormant until you set a verify address. You run the server and write the wording.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you resell or license your app and need to be able to switch it off remotely. Leave the verify address empty and it does nothing.

packages.title: LightSensor
packages.summary: Read the ambient light level around the device, in lux and in simple words like dark or sunlight.
packages.description: Reports how bright the room is, either once or as a stream that only changes when the light really changes. Each reading comes with a plain category such as dark, indoor or sunlight, so you can dim a reader or brighten a screen without choosing your own thresholds. It works on Android; iOS has no public light sensor.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to adapt your screen to the room, for example a night theme or a brighter display in sun. It does not work on iOS, so keep a manual choice for those people.

packages.title: Live Activities
packages.summary: Show live progress on the iPhone Lock Screen and Dynamic Island, and as ongoing notifications on Android.
packages.description: Start, update and end a live activity from your page, for things like a download, a delivery or a timer. On iPhone it appears on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island, and on Android it shows as an ongoing notification. You design the layout as part of your app.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for something that unfolds over minutes or hours and that people want to glance at without opening the app, such as a delivery, a download, a timer or a ride. Do not make it the only way progress is shown.

packages.title: Live Activity updates via OneSignal
packages.summary: Update a running iPhone Live Activity from your server through OneSignal.
packages.description: Connects the Live Activities package to OneSignal so your backend can push new values to an activity that is already running on the Lock Screen. Works with the Live Activities and OneSignal packages and needs both. iOS only.
packages.whenToUse: Include it when your server needs to update a Live Activity that is already running on the Lock Screen, using OneSignal. Skip it if the activity is only ever updated from inside the app.

packages.title: LivePreview
packages.summary: Shows a live, safe, working DSX example inside a document or page.
packages.description: Renders a piece of DSX in a sandbox next to your text, fitted into the column, with a Preview and Code switch and a zoomable detail view. The example can only use what you explicitly grant it and answers from sample data, never from your real app. You supply the source and the sample data.
packages.whenToUse: Use it in documentation, guides or a design review where readers should see and try a component. Do not use it to show real app screens that need your live data.

packages.title: LegacyLocalPush
packages.summary: Keeps the old local push calls working for web pages written for the previous Despia version.
packages.description: Answers the old localpush verbs (send, cronjob, skip, unschedule, schedule and cronjobs) by using the Notify package underneath. Add it when you convert an app whose pages still call those verbs. New apps call Notify directly and do not need it.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when converting an older Despia app whose pages still schedule local notifications with the old calls. For anything new, use the Notify package directly.

packages.title: LegacyLocation
packages.summary: Keeps old location tracking pages working on the new location package.
packages.description: Gives pages written for the earlier Despia version the same start, stop and background tracking calls they used before, and passes each kept point back as the old change event. It builds on the Geo package, which owns the real location features. New apps should call Geo directly and not add this package.
packages.whenToUse: Add it only for a page converted from the earlier Despia version that still uses its location tracking calls. For anything new, use the Geo package instead.

packages.title: LogRocket
packages.summary: Send errors and logs to LogRocket, with optional session replay.
packages.description: Works with the Error and crash reporting package: it hands captured errors and log lines to LogRocket and lets you identify users. Session replay is off by default and only runs when you enable it and the user consents. Needs a LogRocket account and your app ID. iOS and Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it if you already use LogRocket and want captured app errors and logs to show up there. Session replay is optional and stays off unless you enable it and the person agrees.

packages.title: Lottie animations
packages.summary: Play Lottie animations in your screens, such as onboarding art, empty states and success moments.
packages.description: Adds a lottie element you place in your layout with a link to a Lottie JSON file or a bundled animation name. You can set looping, speed and autoplay, and react when it finishes. The web version pauses on the first frame for people who prefer reduced motion. Needs an animation exported as Lottie JSON.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want a vector animation, such as onboarding art, an empty state or a success moment, exported as Lottie JSON. For video or large images use another media element.

packages.title: Maps
packages.summary: Show maps with pins, routes and your user's location.
packages.description: Adds a map element with pins, routes, circles and user location, plus place search, directions, address lookup and map snapshots. iOS uses Apple Maps and needs no key. Android uses Google Maps and needs your Google Maps API key.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app shows places, routes or the person's location on a map, or needs place search, directions, address lookup or a map picture. For a plain address link, opening the system Maps app is simpler.

packages.title: Mapbox
packages.summary: Draw your app's maps with Mapbox styles and tiles.
packages.description: Makes the Maps package draw through the Mapbox Maps SDK, so you can use Mapbox styles. Needs a Mapbox account and your public access token. Without a token the app falls back to the system map. Works with the Maps package.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your maps drawn with Mapbox styles instead of the system map. It has no calls of its own; you choose Mapbox in the Maps settings and add your public token. Without a token the system map is used.

packages.title: MapLibre
packages.summary: Draw your app's maps with the open source MapLibre renderer.
packages.description: Makes the Maps package draw through MapLibre instead of the system map. Needs no key or account and defaults to free public map tiles. You can point it at any MapLibre style, such as a self-hosted or Protomaps style. Works with the Maps package.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want maps that need no API key or vendor account, or when you want to draw your own style, such as a self-hosted or Protomaps one. Skip it if you need routes, regions, circles or the user location layer, which stay with the system map for now.

packages.title: Math formulas
packages.summary: Show math formulas, written in TeX, as properly typeset equations in your app.
packages.description: Draws formulas in markdown text, inline with $...$ or as a centred block with $$, as real typeset math instead of raw TeX source. Use it for study, science or finance content. On iOS it adds the SwiftMath typesetter and about 7 MB of math fonts; the web already shows math with the browser's own layout. Android is not covered yet.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your markdown shows formulas written in TeX, such as study, science or finance content. Skip it if your app never shows math, since it adds about 7 MB of fonts on iOS.

packages.title: MCP
packages.summary: Let AI agents call chosen actions of your app as Model Context Protocol tools.
packages.description: Turns the app into a local Model Context Protocol server, so an AI agent can call the actions you have chosen to expose. Each package opts its own actions in, and any that change something need approval. On desktop, an outside agent can connect only if the person agrees and the build allows it.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want an AI agent, in the app or on a desktop, to read from or act in your app through tools you control. If you do not want agents to reach your app, leave it out.

packages.title: Photos and videos
packages.summary: Let users pick, crop, save and upload photos and videos.
packages.description: Opens the system photo picker without asking for library access, so there is no permission prompt for the common case. Can also take a photo with the camera, pick documents, crop and resize images, make video thumbnails, save to the library and upload the result. Camera and library permissions are asked only when a feature needs them.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it whenever the user needs to choose, edit, save or upload a photo or video, or when you want to build your own photo grid. For taking a new photo with live camera controls, use the camera package instead.

packages.title: MenuBar
packages.summary: A native bottom menu bar and a slide-over sidebar that your web page controls.
packages.description: Shows a bottom bar of icons and labels, and a sidebar that slides over the screen, using the system look including Liquid Glass on iOS 26. Your page gives the items and gets an event when one is tapped, and it decides what the tap means. The bar also tells your page how much room it takes so you can leave space.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when a web-based app needs a real native menu at the bottom or a slide-in side menu. If you build your screens in DSX, use the tab bar or navigation components instead.

packages.title: Sign in with Facebook
packages.summary: Let people sign in to your iOS app with Facebook.
packages.description: Adds a Facebook option using Meta's Limited Login, which returns a token your account service verifies and does not track people across apps. The build sets up the Facebook entries your app needs. Needs a Meta app with its App ID and client token. Works on iOS.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want a Sign in with Facebook button on iOS. Your account service must verify the token it returns, since this package only collects it. Skip it if your people do not use Facebook.

packages.title: Meta App Events
packages.summary: Report app events and purchases to Meta ads, match them to people, and open Meta deferred app links.
packages.description: Starts the Meta SDK only after the person has agreed, sends app events and purchases to Meta so your ads can be measured and optimised, cleans and hashes customer details for matching, and reads the deferred app link of a Meta ad. Works alone or as a destination of the analytics package. Needs your Meta app id and client token. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you buy ads on Facebook or Instagram and want Meta to measure and optimise them from in-app events. Skip it if you do not advertise on Meta.
packages.nativeValue: Meta's native SDK reports installs, app events and purchases with the signals a web page cannot read, and returns the deferred app link of a Meta ad.

actions.name: logEvent

packages.title: MetaConversions
packages.summary: Send your app's conversion events to Meta ads from your own server.
packages.description: Takes a Growth event on your server, checks that the person agreed to attribution and sharing with Meta, hashes their contact details and sends the event to the Meta Conversions API. It answers with whether it was sent and a record of the decision. You need a Meta dataset id and an access token, and nothing can call it from a device.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to report sign-ups, purchases and other conversions to Meta for ad measurement. It only runs on your server and only sends events for people who have given consent.

packages.title: Mixpanel
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to Mixpanel.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it takes the events it collects and delivers them to your Mixpanel project, tied to the signed-in user or an anonymous id. Use it when your team analyses behaviour in Mixpanel. Needs a Mixpanel account and your project token.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your team analyses behaviour in Mixpanel. Pick it as the Growth destination, and use another destination package if you use a different tool.

packages.title: Motion sensors
packages.summary: Read accelerometer, gyroscope, steps and activity from the device.
packages.description: Streams motion sensor data at the rate you choose, and reads the barometer, step count and activity type such as walking or driving. Use it for fitness, games and gesture features. Asks for motion permission when needed, with text you set. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for fitness, games, gestures and movement-aware features that need motion data at a rate you choose. For a one-off compass or orientation reading on a page, the browser sensors may be enough.
packages.nativeValue: Native sampling supports configurable rates and sensor selection. Android can keep a session active with an opt-in foreground service; iOS suspends live callbacks. Native batches can be posted to an app-owned server.

actions.name: activity
actions.description: Starts or stops classification of what the person is doing, such as walking, running, cycling or driving.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to adapt the app to movement, for example to hush notifications while driving. It is not available in the browser.

params.name: activities
params.description: Transition activity filter, default all five. iOS emits initial enter for active flags, then enter/exit changes. Android also supports onFoot transitions; iOS rejects that class with unsupported_platform.

params.name: intervalMillis
params.description: Android default 10000 requested classification interval. iOS default native cadence; an explicit value throttles delivery. 0 requests fastest delivery. Ignored in transition mode.

params.name: mode
params.description: Default classification. Transitions uses Google Transition API on Android and edges of CoreMotion independent activity flags on iOS.

params.name: on
params.description: True starts the classification and false stops it.

params.name: prompt
params.description: True lets the system permission dialog appear on this call when it can; false never shows it and fails if access is missing.

params.name: transitions
params.description: Default enter and exit. Select transition directions in transition mode.

packages.title: Mount
packages.summary: Places a component or a piece of markup over your screen or web page and tells you how much space it uses.
packages.description: Mounts any imported component, such as an ad banner, over a DSX screen or a web page, on the edge you choose. The package hands back the space it takes as CSS insets so your layout can make room. You write the markup or page that hosts the mount and the CSS that uses the insets.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to put a banner, bar or overlay from another package on top of a screen or web page without hand-placing it. Do not use it for normal page content, which belongs in your own layout.

packages.title: Mux Data
packages.summary: Measure how well your videos play with Mux Data.
packages.description: Sends what your video elements already measure, such as startup time, rebuffering, quality changes, pauses and watch progress, to Mux Data. Use it to see playback quality across devices. Needs a Mux account and your Mux Data environment key. iOS and Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want to see how well your videos play across devices, with startup time, rebuffering and quality changes in Mux Data. It reports what the video element already measures; it does not change playback. Skip it if you do not use Mux.

packages.title: Nearby
packages.summary: Connect two phones running your app directly and send them data, with no server.
packages.description: Discover nearby peers, approve encrypted connections, exchange bytes, files and streams. Google Nearby transport supports iOS and Android; iOS Multipeer is also selectable.
packages.whenToUse: Local multiplayer, classroom or file sharing. Select transport:nearby on both sides for iOS/Android links; match serviceId and strategy. Authenticate peers before respond.

actions.description: Starts one nearby session with explicit invitation approval, discovery metadata and file/stream lifecycle events.
actions.whenToUse: Start on a nearby screen. Use transport:nearby on both devices for iOS/Android communication, or the iOS Multipeer default for Apple-only peers.

params.description: Google advertising low-power option on Android and iOS Nearby. Default false. Multipeer rejects.

params.name: approval
params.description: Manual emits invitation and waits for respond; automatic explicitly trusts every peer. Service id is public discovery, never authentication. Default manual.

params.name: autoUpgradeBandwidth
params.description: iOS Google public adapter autoUpgradeBandwidth. Default true; Android 19.4.0 and Multipeer reject this selector.

params.description: Android connected-device foreground service. Default false. Start while visible; stop releases it. iOS rejects true with unsupported_platform.

params.description: Emit Android BandwidthInfo callback events; default true on Android. iOS has no quality callback and rejects this selector when supplied.

params.name: connectionType
params.description: Android AdvertisingOptions.setConnectionType. iOS rejects this selector. Default balanced.

params.name: discoveryLowPower
params.description: Google discovery low-power option on Android and iOS Nearby. Default false. Multipeer rejects.

params.name: enableBLEV2
params.description: iOS Google legacy BLEv2 selector, default true. The pinned SDK always enables BLEv2 and its deprecated setter is a no-op; false rejects unsupported_platform. Omit ble from mediums to exclude BLE. Android and Multipeer reject this selector.

params.name: enableWifiAware
params.description: iOS Google public wifiAwareEnabled flag. Default false, reset for each session; Android and Multipeer reject.

params.name: enforceTopologyConstraints
params.description: iOS Google public adapter enforceTopologyConstraints. Default false; Android 19.4.0 and Multipeer reject this selector.

params.name: mediums
params.description: iOS Google Nearby medium allowlist. Default all SDK media. Android and Multipeer reject this selector. Availability remains controlled by SDK/OS.

params.name: metadata
params.description: Public discovery string map. At most 16 entries, UTF-8 keys 1–32 bytes, values <=256 bytes, total <=1024 bytes. Nearby encodes name + metadata + context as <=131 UTF-8 bytes; oversized requests fail invalid_argument. Multipeer TXT keys cannot contain = and each UTF-8 key=value must fit 255 bytes.

params.name: mode
params.description: Whether to advertise, discover or do both. Defaults to both.

params.name: name
params.description: The name other devices see for this one. Defaults to the device name.

params.name: notificationText
params.description: Android background notification. Default Sharing with a nearby device. Requires background:true; iOS rejects this selector.

params.name: notificationTitle
params.description: Android background notification. Default Nearby connection. Requires background:true; iOS rejects this selector.

params.name: prompt
params.description: Set to false to fail with permission_denied instead of showing the system permission dialog.

params.name: strategy
params.description: Google topology (both peers must match); Multipeer accepts mesh only. Default star for nearby; mesh for multipeer.

params.name: transport
params.description: Protocol on the wire; both peers must select the same protocol. multipeer is iOS only. Default multipeer on iOS; nearby on Android.

packages.title: Net
packages.summary: Know what kind of connection the device has and whether your app can really reach the internet.
packages.description: Tells your app whether the device is online, whether the link is wifi or cellular, whether it is metered or in data saver mode, and can run a real round trip to check that your backend answers. The same facts are also available as live variables you can bind to a layout, so a banner can appear when the connection drops.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to show an offline banner, hold back big downloads on a metered link, or check that your backend is reachable before a sync. You rarely need to call it, since the variables update on their own.

packages.title: NFC tags
packages.summary: Read and write NFC tags from your app.
packages.description: Reads NDEF tags and writes a text record to them. Needs the NFC Tag Reading capability enabled on your Apple App ID and a phone that supports NFC. It is off by default and you turn it on when you want it.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app should read an NFC tag the user holds to the phone, or write a short text onto one, for example for check-ins, product tags or pairing. It reads and writes text tags only, and needs a phone with NFC.
packages.nativeValue: Reading tags uses the phone's own NFC scan sheet, which a web page cannot open on iPhone.

packages.title: Push notifications
packages.summary: Receive and show push and local notifications in your app without a third-party push SDK.
packages.description: Handles the notification permission, the device token, Android channels, action buttons, badges, images, scheduled notifications and what happens when a user taps one. Use it when you want notifications built in rather than through OneSignal or Firebase. You send pushes from your own server with your own Apple push key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs to remind, alert or message people outside the app, from your own server or from the device itself. If you already use a push vendor, keep it and use this package only for the local side.
packages.nativeValue: Web pages cannot reliably show notifications, set a badge or keep action buttons when the app is closed. Native notifications give you the system permission flow, app-icon badges, Android channels and reply buttons.

packages.title: OAuth
packages.summary: Sign users in with Google, Apple, GitHub or any other OAuth provider in the system sign-in sheet.
packages.description: Opens your provider's sign-in page in the trusted system browser sheet and hands you back every value the provider sent to your redirect address, such as the code or the tokens. It checks the state value for you and can create and redeem a PKCE challenge. You write the authorize address and exchange the code with your own backend or the provider.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for social or enterprise sign-in with providers that refuse to load inside an embedded web view. If you only need a native Apple or Google button, use that provider's own package instead.
packages.nativeValue: The system sign-in sheet shares the user's existing browser sessions, so people are often already signed in, and providers that block embedded web views accept it.

packages.title: OneSignal
packages.summary: Send push notifications to your app's users through OneSignal.
packages.description:
Registers the device with OneSignal, asks for notification permission and links each device to your signed-in user, so you can send pushes from the OneSignal dashboard. Use it when your team already runs its messaging on OneSignal. Needs a OneSignal account and your OneSignal App ID.

## Set it up

1. Create an app in the [OneSignal dashboard](https://onesignal.com) and add your Apple push key and Firebase project.
2. Add **OneSignal** and paste your **OneSignal App ID**.
3. Build the app. The first launch registers the device; the permission prompt shows when your app asks for it.

## Settings

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| OneSignal App ID | Your OneSignal application ID |
| Push enabled | Turns OneSignal push on or off |
| Open deeplink in browser | Opens a tapped notification's link in Safari instead of the app |
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your team already sends push, email and text messages from OneSignal and you want devices linked to your signed-in people. If you do not use OneSignal, use the plain notifications package.
packages.nativeValue: Uses the real OneSignal SDK and the system push permission, so delivery, opt-in state and background handling are handled the native way.

packages.title: Orientation
packages.summary: Lock or unlock the screen orientation while the app runs.
packages.description: Lets a screen lock portrait or landscape while it is shown and return to the app's normal setting when it leaves, for example a video that goes fullscreen sideways. You can lock from code or declare it on a screen, and read the live orientation and changes. You choose which orientations the app is built to allow.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when a screen needs a fixed orientation, such as fullscreen video, a camera or a game. If the whole app is always portrait, set that once at build time instead.

packages.title: Passkeys
packages.summary: Sign people in with passkeys from the phone's own authenticator, with any backend.
packages.description: Create a passkey and sign in with one using the system passkey sheet on iOS, Android and the web. You get the raw response to send to your own server, which verifies it against the challenge it issued. The package does not store credentials or verify them for you. You need your own sign-in server and a domain set up for passkeys.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for passwordless sign-in when you run your own backend or use a service that accepts standard WebAuthn responses. If you already use Clerk, use its own package instead.

packages.title: Pay
packages.summary: Take payments with the Apple Pay and Google Pay sheet.
packages.description: Shows the native wallet sheet or a native wallet button and hands you the payment token to send to your own payment processor. The package never sees, stores or forwards the token, and it checks that your line items add up to the total. You need a payment processor, an Apple merchant id for iOS, and Google Pay gateway details for Android.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for a one-tap checkout with the wallet the customer already trusts. If you only need card entry, use the Stripe package instead.

packages.title: Payments
packages.summary: Take payments in your app with one set of calls, whichever payment provider you use.
packages.description: Gives your app one way to start a payment, manage saved cards, link a bank account and open a customer portal, drawn by the payment package you add, such as Stripe. Add the provider packages you need and nothing more. Needs an account with that provider.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to take payments inside your app through one set of calls, whichever provider package you add. Choose it before wiring a provider's own calls, so you can change provider later. Do not use it for in-app purchases of digital goods, which belong to the stores.
packages.nativeValue: Native payment sheets support Apple Pay and Google Pay, saved cards and bank linking with the operating system's own look, and card numbers go straight to the provider.

packages.title: Permissions
packages.summary: Find out which permissions your app build is allowed to ask for, so you can hide features it can never turn on.
packages.description: Reads the permissions declared inside the installed app, such as camera, microphone or location, and gives you the list in one common vocabulary on iOS and Android. You use it to hide buttons for features the build cannot support, instead of prompting and getting a silent refusal. It does not ask the person for anything.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when a screen should only show a feature if the build can request that permission. It lists what the app may ask for, not what the person has granted, so use the permission actions of each feature package for the person's answer.

packages.title: Persona
packages.summary: Verify your users' identity with Persona's checks inside your app.
packages.description: Opens Persona's identity verification flow from a template you set up, or resumes one your server created, and tells your app when the person finishes or leaves. Your server reads the real result with your Persona API key. iOS and Android only. Needs a Persona account, plus camera permission text.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you must confirm who a person is with a government ID and a selfie, for example for finance or age checks. The result on the device is only a report; your server must read the real verdict from Persona.

packages.title: Plaid
packages.summary: Let users link their bank account with Plaid.
packages.description: Opens Plaid Link so a user can pick their bank and connect it, and tells your app whether they finished or cancelled. Your server creates the link token and receives the result. Works with the Payments package. Needs a Plaid account.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your server needs the user to connect a bank account, for example to check balances or start bank payments. Your server creates the link token and swaps the result for an access token; the app never does either.

packages.title: Platform
packages.summary: Despia's own hosted platform backend, written in DSX, kept as a working example of a full server.
packages.description: A server written entirely in DSX that runs Despia's hosted platform: its data, routes, workers and actions are declared and compiled like any other package. It runs on Cloudflare Workers with a Postgres database and a build runner, without naming any of them in the code. It is for reading and learning from, not something you add to an app.
packages.whenToUse: Read it as an example of a full DSX backend. Do not add it to your own app, because it is the backend that runs Despia's hosted platform.

packages.title: Player
packages.summary: Play videos and streams in your app, with offline downloads.
packages.description: A complete video player for your app: the picture, touch controls that hide themselves, a seek bar with chapters, speed, quality, audio and subtitle choices, Picture in Picture and offline copies. You can put the player inside a screen like any other element, or open it full screen with one call. You write the video addresses, titles and the screens around the player.
packages.whenToUse: Use it whenever the app plays a video or a streamed playlist, inline in a card or full screen. For plain audio, use the audio package instead.

packages.title: Content policy
packages.summary: Set your own rules for what users may send, and flag, hold or block anything that breaks them.
packages.description: You load rules written as data, such as words to flag or limits to enforce, and each decision is recorded. With the Chat package, every message sent or received is checked, and blocked messages are refused or hidden. It ships with no rules of its own, so you write them.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when you need rules about what people may send, such as flagging payment requests or blocking abuse. It comes with no rules, so you write the packs; with the Chat package every message is checked. For one-off moderation of your own content you could just write the check in your app.

packages.title: Postgres
packages.summary: Store your server data in a Postgres database with row-level security.
packages.description: Connects your server to a Postgres database, such as the one behind Supabase, and builds the tables, indexes and per-user access rules from the data you declare. There is nothing to call from the app. You provide the database address in the server settings.
packages.whenToUse: Choose it when your server needs a real relational database with per-user row access rules. It runs only on your server, and the app never talks to it directly.

packages.title: PostHog
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to PostHog.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it takes the events it collects and delivers them to your PostHog project. PostHog accepts events without confirming it kept them, so check its activity view when you first connect. Needs a PostHog account and your project key.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you analyse your product in PostHog. It sends the events your app already records to your PostHog project; you do not call it yourself.

actions.name: send
actions.description: Sends a batch of recorded events to your PostHog project in one request. The product analytics package calls it for you.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not call it directly; record events through the product analytics package.

packages.title: PostHog
packages.summary: Sends your app's error and crash reports to PostHog.
packages.description: Delivers each batch of telemetry to your PostHog project as exception events, so crashes appear in PostHog error tracking, with repeated crashes counted as one issue. Needs a PostHog project token, and you choose the PostHog host if you do not use the default.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your team already tracks product analytics in PostHog and wants crashes there too. For your own server, use the Http destination instead.

packages.title: PreventDefault
packages.summary: Control keyboard-driven layout adjustment.
packages.description: Suppress keyboard-driven layout adjustment while a screen manages its own layout. The result reports whether suppression is in force.
packages.whenToUse: Use when a screen manages its own keyboard avoidance.

actions.name: autoscroll
actions.description: Turns the native iOS keyboard autoscroll off, or back on. Called with no value it prevents autoscroll. The default at launch is autoscroll restored.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Describes the native behavior: true restores iOS autoscroll, false or omitted prevents it.

packages.title: Preview
packages.summary: Turn a pasted web link into a preview card with title, description and picture.
packages.description: Fetches a web page and gives you its title, description, main image, site name, icon and canonical address, decided by one consistent set of rules on every platform. It reads the page once, runs no scripts from it and caches nothing. You draw the card and decide whether to keep the result.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when someone pastes a link into a chat, note or bookmark list and you want a preview card. For a full web page view, open the link instead.

packages.title: PrintDocuments
packages.summary: Print a PDF or other document through the system print sheet.
packages.description: Presents the system print sheet for a file in your app or for a web address it downloads first, and tells you whether printing went ahead. The person picks the printer and options in the system sheet. You supply the document and a job name.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for receipts, tickets, reports and other documents the person may want on paper. For sharing a file rather than printing it, use the share sheet.
packages.nativeValue: The native print sheet finds nearby AirPrint and system printers and shows the real preview and options, which a web page's print dialog does not.

actions.name: document

params.name: anchor
params.description: The on-screen element the print UI relates to, in window points; a call from a mounted surface passes the element rect in that surface's coordinates and the surface owner converts it. Where the platform presents a popover (iPad, Mac) its arrow points at this rectangle; full-screen sheets on phones, Android and browsers have no anchor. Default: the window center. A rectangle without finite numbers and a positive size rejects invalid_argument on every platform. Applies at call.

params.name: androidHtmlPrintAdapter
params.description: Deprecated, kept for existing callers. HTML and text documents already use the system web engine's paged print layout on every platform, supplied by the print content formatter. true keeps that default; false makes Android lay HTML out on the canvas path instead. Accepted on every platform; it changes nothing outside Android. With render, true rejects unsupported_platform on Android because that layout cannot be captured into a file. Applies at call.

packages.title: DomPrintDocuments
packages.summary: Optional HTML and text formatter for PrintDocuments.
packages.description: Adds the platform web engine as the HTML and text formatter for PrintDocuments on iOS, Android and Mac. File printing remains independent of this package.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your app prints HTML or text. Printing files, web addresses and images works without it, so leave it out of apps that never print HTML.

packages.title: Push to talk
packages.summary: Add walkie-talkie voice channels where people hold a button to speak.
packages.description: One person holds a button and talks while everyone on the channel hears them live, and nobody else can speak until they let go. Works with the Calls package. Needs a call provider and a floor service with a token endpoint.
packages.whenToUse: Add it for walkie-talkie style channels where one person speaks at a time, such as a team on a job site. For normal calls where everyone talks together, use the Calls package.

packages.title: PullToRefresh
packages.summary: Let people pull down on a web page in your app to reload it.
packages.description: Adds the familiar pull-down-to-refresh control to the web page your app shows, with a spinner whose colours you can set for light and dark. It reloads the page, and you can also start a refresh from code. Screens built with DSX use the native refreshable element instead.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app shows a web page and people expect to pull down to refresh it. For native DSX screens use the refreshable element instead.
packages.nativeValue: It uses the native overscroll gesture and spinner, so it feels like the rest of the phone.

packages.title: PushRouting
packages.summary: Delivers the notification a user tapped to your app's pages once they are ready.
packages.description: When a user taps a push notification, this package holds the payload until the page has loaded, then sends it to your app as a notification event and opens any deep-link path. It also queues silent pushes so you can read them later. It works with any push provider; you write the code that reacts to the event.
packages.whenToUse: Listen to its events when you want to react to a tapped notification or to a silent push. You do not need to call it yourself for ordinary tap routing, it runs on every page load.

packages.title: QuickActions
packages.summary: Add shortcuts to your app icon's long-press menu on the Home screen.
packages.description: Lets you set the shortcuts that appear when someone presses and holds your app icon, each with a title, an icon and a value. When one is chosen the app opens and your code is told which value was picked, whether the app was closed or already running. You choose the items and decide what each one does.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to give quick routes into your app, such as New message or Scan, from the Home screen icon. The shortcuts are shown by the system, so keep them few and short.
packages.nativeValue: The shortcuts live in the system's icon menu, outside your app, and work even when the app is not running.

packages.title: Record
packages.summary: Record a voice note or audio message and get the file back, with a live level meter.
packages.description: Starts, pauses, resumes and stops a microphone recording, and can also record a bus or input of the Audio package's live graph. You get a level meter while recording, a file in the format you choose, and a clean recovery when a call or another app interrupts. You write your own record button, meter and save or discard screen.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for voice notes, audio messages, pronunciation practice and field capture. For multitrack editing or mixing use the Edit package instead.

packages.title: Firebase Remote Config
packages.summary: Change app settings and switch features off without releasing a new version.
packages.description: Fetches values from Firebase Remote Config, caches them and lets your screens react to them, so you can turn off a broken feature or stage a rollout. You set safe default values for when the device is offline. Needs your Firebase project set up in the app.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to switch off a broken feature, stage a rollout or change a banner without publishing a new build. Always set defaults first so the app behaves safely when the server cannot be reached. Do not use it for private data, since the values are not secret.

packages.title: RemoteHosts
packages.summary: Move your app to a new domain without shipping a new app version.
packages.description: Lets the app refresh its list of web hosts from a file you control, so you can change domains without an App Store rebuild. It is off until your app settings give a refresh address, and if the fetch fails the bundled hosts stay in use. You host the file and edit it when you migrate.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you may need to change the domain your app loads from, for example during a rebrand or a client move. If your domain will never change you can leave it out.

packages.title: RevenueCat
packages.summary: Sell subscriptions and in-app purchases with RevenueCat.
packages.description: Lets your pages start a purchase, open a RevenueCat paywall or the customer center, and read products, offerings, purchase history and what a user is entitled to. Use it when your team already manages subscriptions in RevenueCat. Needs a RevenueCat account and its iOS and Android API keys.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your team already manages subscriptions and in-app purchases in RevenueCat and you want the app to buy, show paywalls and read entitlements. If you sell through the stores directly without RevenueCat, use the store purchase package instead.
packages.nativeValue: Purchases run through StoreKit and Google Play Billing, which a web page cannot reach, and RevenueCat's native paywall and customer center come with it.

packages.title: RevenueCat
packages.summary: Sell subscriptions and in-app purchases with RevenueCat.
packages.description: Lets your pages start a purchase, open a RevenueCat paywall or the customer center, and read products, offerings, purchase history and what a user is entitled to. Use it when your team already manages subscriptions in RevenueCat. Needs a RevenueCat account and its iOS and Android API keys.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your subscriptions and in-app purchases are managed in RevenueCat and you want one call to sell, show a paywall and check what a person owns. Do not include it next to the standalone RevenueCat package, since an app uses one or the other.
packages.nativeValue: Purchases run through the real App Store and Google Play billing sheets, and the paywall and customer center are RevenueCat's own native screens.

packages.title: Rive animations
packages.summary: Add interactive Rive animations that react to your app's data and send events back.
packages.description: Adds a rive element that plays a .riv file from a link or the app bundle. Its state machine inputs can follow your app's variables, so an animated cart or onboarding figure changes as the data does, and animation events can trigger actions in your app. Use it when you need animation that responds, rather than one that only plays. Needs a .riv file made in Rive.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want an animated figure that reacts to your data, such as an onboarding character, an animated cart or a game-like control, and your designer works in Rive. For a plain looping graphic an image or video is simpler.

packages.title: RudderStack
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to your RudderStack data plane.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it delivers the events it collects to RudderStack, so you can route them on to your other tools. Delivery onward from RudderStack is not visible to the app. Needs a RudderStack source write key and the address of your data plane, cloud or self-hosted.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your analytics events should flow into RudderStack, either RudderStack Cloud or a data plane you host yourself. Skip it if you send events to another destination, or if you cannot give it your own data plane address.

packages.title: Scanner
packages.summary: Scan QR codes, barcodes and paper documents with the camera.
packages.description: Opens the phone's own scanner to read a QR code or barcode, or to scan a paper document into pages with the text read off them. It also gives you a scanner preview you can place inside your own layout. QR and barcode scanning stay free.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when people need to scan a QR code, a barcode or a paper document. If you want your own camera screen with scanning on top, use the scanner preview in your layout instead.
packages.nativeValue: It uses the system scanners, VisionKit on iOS and Google's scanner on Android, which are fast and handle focus and edge detection for you.

actions.name: scan
actions.description: Opens the system scanner for a code or a document and resolves with what was read. Backing out resolves as cancelled.
actions.whenToUse: Use it for a one-off scan, such as a ticket or a receipt.

packages.title: Scene
packages.summary: Inspect and control the 3D scenes on screen from code, markup or an AI agent.
packages.description: Lets any action, or an AI agent through the MCP package, look at the nodes of a mounted scene, change their attributes, move the camera, take a picture, test what is under a point and read collisions and statistics. It adds no screen of its own and works on the scene elements you already have.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want to change or inspect a 3D scene while the app runs, for testing, debugging or letting an AI agent drive the scene. To build the scene itself, use the scene markup elements.

packages.title: 3D models and AR
packages.summary: Show 3D models people can spin and zoom, and place them in the real world with AR.
packages.description: Adds a Scene3D element that displays a 3D model (USDZ, .reality or glTF) from a link, with orbit, pinch zoom, a turntable spin and model animations. With the AR package it can also place the model on a floor or wall, try it on a face, attach it to an image, or work as a tape measure. Good for product viewers. Needs your 3D files hosted online.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for product viewers, hero models and simple augmented reality placement. Do not use it for games or physics, which need a game engine package.

packages.title: Screenshot protection
packages.summary: Hide your app's content in screenshots and screen recordings, and find out when someone tries.
packages.description: Blanks the app in screenshots and screen recordings and tells your screens when a capture is attempted, so you can blur sensitive content or warn the person. Use it for banking, health or private content. It only works while the screen capture prevention setting in the Security package is on. On Android versions before 14 it blocks capture without the notice.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for banking, health or private content that should not appear in screenshots or screen recordings, or when you want to warn the person that a capture was attempted. It only works while the screen capture prevention setting in the Security package is on.

packages.title: Spotlight
packages.summary: Make your app's content findable from the phone's own search, and open the right screen when it is tapped.
packages.description: Adds your items, such as recipes or notes, to Spotlight on Apple devices and to system search on Android, so people can find them from outside your app. Tapping a result opens the screen you named for it. You choose which items to add, and you remove them when the person signs out.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app has content people search for, such as recipes, contacts, documents or products. Do not add private content unless the person expects it to appear in system search, and clear it on sign-out.

packages.title: Security
packages.summary: Switch on app security policies such as blocking jailbroken devices and screenshots.
packages.description: Holds the security settings for your app: refuse to run on jailbroken devices, reject invalid TLS certificates and block screenshots and screen recording. It has no actions to call, you choose each policy in settings. Each one is off until you turn it on.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for banking, health or other sensitive apps that must protect their screens and connections. Leave policies off for ordinary apps, since blocking screenshots or rooted devices can frustrate honest users.

packages.title: Segment
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to Segment.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it delivers the events it collects to Segment, which can pass them to your other tools. Segment accepts events without confirming it kept them, so check its Debugger when you first connect. Needs a Segment source write key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you already use Segment and want your app's analytics events delivered there. Pick it as the destination in the product analytics settings. Do not rely on it to confirm delivery, because Segment accepts events first and rejects some later.

packages.title: Sentry
packages.summary: Send your app's errors and crash reports to your own Sentry project.
packages.description: Takes the errors the error reporting package has already captured and cleaned up, and sends each batch straight to your Sentry project over HTTPS. Nothing passes through Despia. You need a Sentry project and its DSN, and the error reporting package does the capturing.
packages.whenToUse: Use it if your team already uses Sentry and you want app errors to land there. It only sends what the error reporting package captured.

packages.title: Server
packages.summary: The backend settings for your app: sign-in, data, address and where it is deployed.
packages.description: Holds the settings for your app's own backend, such as how logins are checked, which database it uses, the address the app talks to, the deploy target and request limits. It also lets other packages mark an action to run on your server instead of the phone. It adds no commands of its own. You fill in the settings and the packages that need a server use them.
packages.whenToUse: Include it when your app has its own backend and you want to set its login checking, database and deploy target in one place. If your app has no server code, you do not need it.

packages.title: AppSettings
packages.summary: Open your app's page in the system Settings.
packages.description: Sends the user to this app's page in the Settings app, or to a deeper page such as notifications, so they can switch back on a permission they denied earlier. The phone will not show the system prompt a second time, so this is the way back. It does not wait for the user to return. You write the button and the explanation around it.
packages.whenToUse: Use it from a button the user taps after a permission was denied, such as notifications or location. Do not call it automatically, and note that it cannot change a setting for the user.
packages.nativeValue: Only the native app can open the system Settings page for itself; a web page has no way to.

packages.title: Share sheet
packages.summary: Let people share text, links and files from your app through the phone's share sheet.
packages.description: Opens the native share sheet so users can send to Messages, Mail, WhatsApp, AirDrop, Files or copy to the clipboard. You can share a message, a link and attachments from your app's files together. No account or keys needed.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when the user wants to send something out of your app, such as a link, a message or a file, through whichever app they choose. It does not post to a specific network for you.
packages.nativeValue: The user gets the real system share sheet with their own apps and contacts, and files go as true attachments.

actions.name: present
actions.description: Opens the system share sheet with text, a link and files, and resolves when the user shares or closes it.
actions.whenToUse: Call it from a share button. Closing the sheet is a normal answer, reported as completed false, not an error.

packages.title: Watch together
packages.summary: Let people watch or listen together with playback in sync.
packages.description: Two or more people open the same video, song or document. One person presses play and everyone follows, and anyone who joins late catches up. Shares a members list and one state. Needs a session service address.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for watch-together, listen-together or shared-document features where everyone sees the same state and the same playback position. It does not draw a members list or a call screen; you build those from the package context.

packages.title: SharePlay
packages.summary: Start shared sessions from FaceTime with SharePlay.
packages.description: Works with the Watch together package. Inside a FaceTime call or from the share sheet, people join with one tap. Needs the Group Activities capability on your app ID. iOS only.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when people should watch or work together inside a FaceTime call, with one tap to join. It only carries the shared session, so you start it with the shared session calls. It does nothing on Android or the web.

packages.title: ShareExtension
packages.summary: Lets people share text, links, photos and files into your app from the system share sheet.
packages.description: Adds your app to the share sheet on iPhone, Mac and Android and to the Open with list on desktop. Everything shared is saved safely in an inbox until your app takes it, even if the app was closed. You write what the app does with each shared item.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when people should be able to send things to your app from other apps, such as saving a link or uploading a photo. Do not use it if your app only needs to share content out.

packages.title: LegacySiri
packages.summary: Let people add a spoken Siri phrase that opens your app and tells it what to do.
packages.description: Shows the system Add to Siri sheet for a phrase you choose. When the person later says the phrase, the app opens and receives a trigger event with the phrase and any data you attached. This keeps the older add to Siri behavior working for apps that already use it. It works on iOS only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to keep an existing phrase-based Siri shortcut working. For new apps, declare assistant tools instead, which Siri and other assistants can discover without the person recording a phrase.

packages.title: SnapConversions
packages.summary: Send purchases and sign-ups to Snapchat as conversions, from your server.
packages.description: Takes one tracked event and sends it to the Snap Conversions API, with email and phone hashed first and only when the person agreed. It runs on your own server and tells you whether the event was sent, skipped or refused. You supply your Snap token and ids, and may map your own events to Snap events.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to report conversions to Snapchat so your Snap campaigns can be measured, such as a confirmed purchase. Call it from your server only; it has no public route and sends nothing without recorded consent.

packages.title: SpeechRecognition
packages.summary: Turn the user's speech into text with the standard web speech API.
packages.description: Adds the browser SpeechRecognition API to your web pages inside the app, because the iOS and Android web views do not have it, and also offers a simple start, stop and abort call. It listens through the microphone, streams interim and final transcripts, and asks for speech and microphone permission the first time. You write the page that shows the text.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for dictation, voice search or voice commands in a web page. Code written for the standard speech recognition API keeps working without changes.
packages.nativeValue: It uses the phone's own speech recognizer and permission flow, which the web views do not expose.

packages.title: SpeechSynthesis
packages.summary: Speaks text aloud with the device voices, or turns text into audio files.
packages.description: Lists the voices installed on the device, speaks text with a chosen voice, speed, pitch and volume, and reports progress word by word. It can also render speech into audio files that your app keeps. You write the text and decide when to speak or stop.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to read content aloud, give spoken feedback or make audio from text. For recorded or streamed audio, use the audio packages instead.
packages.nativeValue: Native speech uses the high quality system voices, can be turned into files, and plays correctly alongside other audio. The browser voices vary by device and cannot produce files.
