packages.title: Splash
packages.summary: The launch screen shown while your app starts, with your logo and background.
packages.description: Shows your logo and background color the moment the app opens, then hands over to your app once it is ready and the first frame has settled. You can set the minimum time it stays up, the fade, the spinner and the logo size. If the customizable splash is turned off or its settings are invalid, the standard launch screen is used. You provide the logo and colors.
packages.whenToUse: It is always part of the app. Use its settings to match the launch screen to your brand; the minimum time only keeps the splash up longer, it never delays your app's start.

packages.title: Key-value storage
packages.summary: Save small settings and values on the device so they are still there next time the app opens.
packages.description: A simple store for things like a theme choice, a language or a last-seen date. Values keep their type: a number comes back a number. Read or write one value or many at once in a single call, list keys by prefix a page at a time, and every change is announced so two screens never disagree. Values stay on the device, with no account or keys needed.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to remember small things between launches, such as a theme, a language or the last screen. It is not meant for large files or secrets; use files for big data and a secure store for credentials.
packages.nativeValue: Values live in the app's own native storage, so they stay put across launches and keep their type.

packages.title: In-app purchases and paywalls
packages.summary: Sell subscriptions and purchases with a native paywall and one simple way to check what a user owns.
packages.description: Shows a paywall you design in JSON, runs checkout, restores purchases and tells you which entitlements a user has, in the same shape on every platform. It works through Apple StoreKit 2 or RevenueCat. Use it for subscriptions, one-time purchases and paid features. Needs products set up in the App Store or Google Play, or a RevenueCat account.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app sells subscriptions or one-off purchases and you want one set of calls for paywall, checkout, restore and what a person owns, on both iOS and Android. If you already run everything in RevenueCat you can pick that as the provider and keep the same calls.
packages.nativeValue: Checkout runs through the real App Store and Google Play payment sheets, and refunds, subscription management and offer codes open the stores' own screens.

packages.title: Stream
packages.summary: Watch your app's logs live from a test device on your own relay.
packages.description: Sends the on-device log, error and diagnostic feed in batches over HTTPS to a relay that you own, so you can watch a test install as it runs. Each session is started after a confirmation, shows a live badge, and can be stopped at any time. It exists only on test builds and never sends data to Despia. You supply the relay and pair the device with a code.
packages.whenToUse: Use it while testing on a real device when you want to follow logs from your desk, or to send a one-off report to yourself. It is not available in App Store builds, and it only talks to a relay you own.

packages.title: Stream Video
packages.summary: Run your app's video calls on Stream.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. Stream carries the audio and video while the Calls package handles ringing and call screens. Needs a Stream account, your API key and a token endpoint on your server.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your calls should run on Stream's video network. You still start, answer and draw calls with the call package; this package supplies the media and Stream-only features such as cloud recording and captions.

packages.title: Stripe
packages.summary: Take card, Apple Pay and bank payments with Stripe.
packages.description: Shows Stripe's payment sheet and customer sheet in your app, supports Apple Pay and optional card scanning, and handles bank payments and Connect onboarding. Your server creates the payments and sends the secrets to the app. Works with the Payments package. Needs a Stripe account, your publishable key and, for Apple Pay, an Apple merchant ID.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to take card, Apple Pay, Google Pay and bank payments through Stripe in a native app. Your own server must create the payment and send its secrets to the app; this package never holds your secret key.
packages.nativeValue: Native Stripe sheets give Apple Pay, Google Pay, card scanning and bank linking that web checkout cannot match, and the payment never leaves your app.

packages.title: Stripe Terminal
packages.summary: Take in-person card payments with Stripe card readers.
packages.description: Finds and connects Bluetooth, internet, USB (Android) or phone-based readers, then collects, confirms and refunds payments your server created. Use it for point of sale and shop counters. Works with the Payments package. Needs a Stripe account, a Stripe location for the reader, and a server endpoint that issues connection tokens.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for in-person card payments with a Stripe card reader, such as a shop counter or a pop-up stand. For payments inside the app with no reader, use the Payments package instead.

packages.title: Terra Health
packages.summary: Pull Apple Health and wearable data into your app through Terra.
packages.description:
Connects Apple Health and wearables such as Fitbit, Garmin, Oura and Whoop through Terra, then syncs and reads the data. Needs a Terra account and developer ID, and your own server to start sessions with Terra's API. It is off by default and you turn it on when you want it.

## How it connects

- **Apple Health** is read on the device through HealthKit. iOS asks the person once, with the purpose strings you set.
- **Wearables** (Fitbit, Garmin, Oura, Whoop and more) connect through Terra's Connect widget, opened from your app.
- **Your server** mints the session token with Terra's API, so your Terra API key never ships in the app.

## Set it up

1. Create a developer account at [Terra](https://tryterra.co) and copy your developer ID.
2. Add **Terra Health** and set **Developer ID**. Leaving it empty keeps the integration off.
3. Write the **Health read prompt** iOS shows when it asks to read Health data.
4. Add a route on your server that asks Terra for a session token for the signed-in user.

| Setting | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Developer ID | Your Terra developer ID |
| Health read prompt | The message iOS shows before reading Health data |
| Health write prompt | The message iOS shows before saving to Health |
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your app should read Apple Health or wearable data (Fitbit, Garmin, Oura, Whoop) and forward it to your own backend through Terra. It needs a Terra account; if you only want Apple Health data inside the app, use the HealthKit package.

packages.title: TikTok Ads
packages.summary: Measure which TikTok ads bring installs and sales, using the TikTok Business SDK.
packages.description: Starts the TikTok Business SDK at launch, records install and purchase events with TikTok, identifies signed-in people with hashed details and fetches the deferred deep link from before the install. It waits for tracking consent when the Consent package is in the build, and also works as a destination for the Product analytics package. Needs a TikTok Ads account, your TikTok app id and an access token, on phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you run TikTok ads and want installs and purchases tied to the campaigns that earned them. Skip it if you do not advertise on TikTok.
packages.nativeValue: The native SDK reads the install referrer and iOS attribution data that a web page cannot, and hashes identity on the device.

packages.title: TikTokEvents
packages.summary: Report purchases and sign-ups to TikTok from your server, only for people who agreed.
packages.description: Sends your conversion events to the TikTok Events API from your own server, with personal details hashed and each send checked against the user's consent. You get an answer saying whether the event was sent, skipped or refused, and why. You provide your TikTok access token and pixel or app id, and call it from server code, never from the app.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you run TikTok ads and want sign-ups, purchases and subscriptions counted for attribution. It only runs on your server, so a device cannot send a fake conversion. Leave it out if you do not advertise on TikTok.

packages.title: Toast
packages.summary: Show short messages and undo bars that disappear on their own.
packages.description: Shows a small card with a message, an optional action button and an icon, which slides in, waits and goes away by itself. The call finishes when the card ends and tells you how: dismissed, the action was tapped, it timed out or it was replaced, so an Undo button needs one line. Cards queue one at a time on phones and lift above the tab bar, a floating button and the keyboard. You write the message text.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for quick feedback such as saved, copied or an Undo after a delete. For a message the person must answer, use a dialog or alert instead.

packages.title: Translate
packages.summary: Translate text between languages, on the device first.
packages.description: Translates text using the phone's own translation models, and detects the source language on Android and the web. If the device cannot do a language pair, it can fall back to your own LibreTranslate-compatible translation service. That service is optional and is set in the settings.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to translate short texts such as chat messages or labels, privately on the device. For long documents or languages the device lacks, point it at your own LibreTranslate-compatible service; it also never translates text that is already in the target language.

packages.title: DeviceUUID
packages.summary: Gives your app a stable anonymous id for each install, with no permission prompt.
packages.description: Returns one identifier that stays the same across launches. It uses the vendor id on iOS, and a generated id kept safely on Android, desktop and the web. It is not an advertising id and cannot be used to fingerprint the device.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to recognise the same install across launches, for example to attach anonymous settings or sessions to a device. Do not use it as an advertising id or for tracking across other companies' apps.
packages.nativeValue: The web can only keep an id in local storage, which is easily cleared. On iOS the vendor id survives reinstalls while any of your apps remains.

packages.title: Stripe Identity
packages.summary: Check who your users are with an ID document and selfie, using Stripe Identity.
packages.description: Opens Stripe Identity's own verification sheet over your app, or a ready-made verify button, and reports whether the person finished, cancelled or failed. Your server reads the final verified result. Works with the Stripe package. Needs a Stripe account with Identity, your publishable key, a server route that creates verification sessions and camera permission text.
packages.whenToUse: Add it when you need to confirm a person's identity with an ID document and selfie, for example before payouts or age checks. It tells your app how the flow ended; your server must read the final verified result, because finishing the flow is not the same as being verified.

packages.title: VerticalPlayerStack
packages.summary: A full-screen vertical video player for short dramas, with paywalls, coins and offline downloads.
packages.description: Presents a swipeable full-screen player for short episodic videos, with a seek bar, speed menu, picture in picture, a paywall and coin unlocks, a Downloads library and a share sheet. You hand it a JSON list of episodes and it streams every viewing event back to your page. You write the episode data and your own server for access and credits.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you are building a short drama or episodic video app in the style of TikTok, with paid episodes and offline viewing. Do not use it for ordinary single-video playback, where a plain video element is enough.

packages.title: Viewport
packages.summary: Keep chat boxes and footers visible when the on-screen keyboard opens.
packages.description: Fixes the common problem where the keyboard covers whatever sits at the bottom of the page. You choose in the settings whether the page shrinks to fit above the keyboard or stays full height while you are told the keyboard height, and the page can switch at runtime. You build any keyboard-aware layout yourself.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for screens with a text field near the bottom, such as a chat composer or a sticky button, so the keyboard does not cover them. Existing apps keep their old behavior until you change the setting.

packages.title: Text recognition and body pose
packages.summary: Read text out of photos and scans, and track body movement from the camera, on the device.
packages.description: Reads the text in an image such as a receipt or a sign, using Apple Vision on iOS and Google ML Kit on Android. It can also follow a person's body joints from the camera or a video, for fitness or movement apps. Images are processed on the device, with no account or API key.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to read text from a photo, receipt or scanned page, or to follow a person's body joints from the camera or a video for fitness and movement features. Do not use it to scan barcodes or documents for their own sake; the Scanner package does that.

packages.title: Wallet
packages.summary: Let people add a boarding pass, ticket or card to Apple Wallet.
packages.description: Downloads a pass file from a web address and shows the system sheet to add it to Apple Wallet on iOS. On Android and the web it hands the pass to the system or browser handler. You host the pass file yourself. Only iOS tells you when the sheet closes.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to offer an Add to Wallet button for a ticket, coupon, loyalty card or boarding pass you already generate as a pass file. It does not create passes.
packages.nativeValue: On iOS the pass is added with Apple's own add-pass sheet, so it lands in the person's real Wallet.

packages.title: Watch
packages.summary: Adds an Apple Watch and Wear OS companion to your app and lets the phone control it.
packages.description: Builds a watch app that shows your own screens, works offline and can be updated over the air. From the phone you can show screens, send state, play haptics and sounds, record, request a location, send notifications and read the battery. You write the watch screens in the same DSX markup as the rest of the app.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app needs a wrist companion that works with the phone. Skip it if you only need notifications mirrored to the watch, which the system already does.

packages.title: WebExtension
packages.summary: Ship a Safari web extension with your app and share state and a sign-in with it.
packages.description: Packages one standard web extension as a Safari extension inside your iOS app and as a zip for the Chrome Web Store. Your app can push values for the extension to read, lend it a revocable sign-in token, hear messages it sends back, and send people to Settings to switch it on. It is off by default; you write the extension's pages and decide what it does.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want your product to live in the browser too, for example to act on pages a user visits while signed in to your app. Skip it if you have no browser-side feature, since it adds an extra target to the app.

packages.title: WebSocket
packages.summary: Connect, reconnect and handle bounded WebSocket queues.
packages.description: Named WebSocket connections with reconnect controls, bounded queues and explicit acknowledgement. Native queues survive relaunch; browser queues last for the current page. Acceptance by the transport does not prove server delivery.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs a live connection to your own server, such as chat, live feeds or presence, and messages must survive a dropped connection or a relaunch. For one-off requests use a normal API call instead.
packages.nativeValue: Native queues persist bounded message records and file handles. Browser queues last for the current page.

actions.name: connect
actions.description: Opens a named connection to a ws:// or wss:// address, or updates it if it is already open, and reconnects automatically if it drops.
actions.whenToUse: Call it once at start-up, and subscribe to the events before you do.

params.name: allowsCellularAccess
params.description: Allows the iOS session to use cellular data. Default true.

params.name: allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess
params.description: Allows the iOS session to use Low Data Mode networks. Default true.

params.name: allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess
params.description: Allows the iOS session to use networks the OS classifies as expensive. Default true.

params.name: caFile
params.description: A Core/Files handle containing one DER CA certificate. Adds this anchor to system trust on native platforms.

params.name: certificatePins
params.description: Lowercase SHA-256 hex hashes of DER server certificates. At least one certificate in a valid server chain must match. Empty uses system trust.

params.name: clientIdentity
params.description: Public alias of an already provisioned system client identity: Keychain label on iOS, user-granted KeyChain alias on Android. Private keys stay in the OS.

params.name: closeTimeout
params.description: Android close handshake deadline in seconds. Default 60.

params.name: compressionThreshold
params.description: Android minimum message bytes for negotiated per-message compression. Default 1024.

params.name: connectTimeout
params.description: Seconds to wait for the opening handshake before failing.

params.name: fastFallback
params.description: Allows Android Happy Eyeballs connection racing. Default true.

params.name: headers
params.description: ASCII HTTP handshake headers on iOS and Android, with token names and no line breaks. Browsers reject this option with unsupported_platform.

params.name: id
params.description: The name you give this connection; use the same name in every later call.

params.name: localNetwork
params.description: Native LAN connection. Android checks or requests the declared local network permission before connecting; iOS uses its first-use system prompt.

params.name: maxBufferedBytes
params.description: Maximum bytes accepted by the transport at once. Default 1048576; send rejects backpressure when the buffer is full.

params.name: maxInboundMessages
params.description: Maximum unacknowledged messages, dropping oldest on overflow. Default 500.

params.name: maxMessageBytes
params.description: Maximum incoming or outgoing frame size in bytes, up to 16777216.

params.name: maxOutboundMessages
params.description: Maximum queued outgoing messages; send rejects queue_full at this limit. Default 500.

params.name: pingInterval
params.description: Native protocol ping interval in seconds, at least 0.001; zero disables pings. Default 25. Browsers have no protocol ping API.

params.name: pingTimeout
params.description: iOS pong deadline in seconds. Default 25. OkHttp uses its ping interval as the pong deadline.

params.name: prompt
params.description: Allow the Android local network prompt for a localNetwork connection. Default true.

params.name: protocols
params.description: The WebSocket subprotocols to offer to the server.

params.name: proxyHost
params.description: Native HTTP CONNECT proxy hostname, without credentials or a URL scheme. Requires proxyPort.

params.name: proxyPort
params.description: Native HTTP CONNECT proxy port from 1 to 65535. Requires proxyHost.

params.name: queueTtl
params.description: Seconds to retain queued messages. Default 604800; expired records are purged before replay, enqueue and status.

params.name: reconnect
params.description: Set to false to turn off automatic reconnecting. It is on by default.

params.name: reconnectBaseDelay
params.description: Initial exponential reconnect delay in seconds.

params.name: reconnectJitter
params.description: Fraction of reconnect delay randomized downward, from zero to one.

params.name: reconnectMaxAttempts
params.description: Reconnect attempt limit; zero allows unlimited retries.

params.name: reconnectMaxDelay
params.description: Maximum reconnect delay in seconds.

params.name: retryOnConnectionFailure
params.description: Allows Android transport route retries within the connection attempt. Default true.

params.name: rid
params.description: A request id the bridge echoes in the events this call causes, for a page that matches replies to its requests.

params.name: url
params.description: The server address, starting with ws:// or wss://.

params.name: waitsForConnectivity
params.description: Allows the iOS session to wait for connectivity within connectTimeout. Default false.

params.name: writeTimeout
params.description: Android socket write deadline in seconds. Default 10.

config.label: Background grace
config.description: Maximum requested iOS grace in seconds, from 0 to 25. Zero disables it; the OS may expire it sooner.

config.label: Background refresh
config.description: iOS opt-in to opportunistic refresh for connections still in memory. The OS decides whether and when to run; process termination needs the app to reconnect.

config.label: Refresh earliest delay
config.description: Minimum seconds before an iOS refresh request becomes eligible; this is not a recurrence guarantee.

config.label: Android LAN permission
config.description: Declares ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK for local servers on supported Android versions. Connect with localNetwork true to request permission just before use.

config.label: Local network explanation
config.description: iOS purpose text for connecting to local servers. Leave empty when no LAN connection is used; every installed package must agree on shared purpose text.

config.label: Scoped transport exceptions
config.description: iOS NSExceptionDomains map. Each lowercase DNS hostname maps to NSIncludesSubdomains, NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads, NSExceptionMinimumTLSVersion and NSExceptionRequiresForwardSecrecy. App Store review may require justification.

packages.title: WebView
packages.summary: Show any web page inside your app.
packages.description: Adds a web view element that embeds a page from a link, with events for start, finish, failure and messages from the page. The page gets no access to native features; it can only send text or JSON back to your app through window.app.send. It is free and open. You decide what to do with each message.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to embed an ordinary web page, such as a checkout, a help page or a map, inside a native UI app screen. It is not the web app shell for hybrid apps, which makes a whole web app native.

packages.title: Home screen widgets
packages.summary: Put your app on the home screen and lock screen with widgets you design in DSX.
packages.description: Each widget is a DSX document that becomes a native iOS WidgetKit widget or an Android Glance widget. Widgets refresh on a schedule, can respond to taps and be configured by the user. Use it to show the next task, a score or a counter at a glance.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when people should see something from your app on the home screen or lock screen without opening it, such as the next task, a score or a counter. Widgets are glanceable; use live activities for something that runs for a few hours.
